articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
articles.summary: When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into…

image.caption: Voyager 1: Destined to wander the Milky Way "eternally"Image: NASA/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.
NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.
But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.
Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.
It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.
How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?
In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.
On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.
In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.
That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.
Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

blocks.caption: There were two Golden Records, one on Voyager 1 and another on Voyager 2, a second spacecraft on the same 1970s mission. They were protected with this gold aluminum cover.Image: United Archives/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment
The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.
"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.
Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1
No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.
We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

articles.title: Judge sets Lindsay Clancy retrial for March in killings of her three children
articles.summary:
Clancy’s first trial on charges of first-degree murder ended in mistrial after jurors couldn’t reach unanimous verdict

A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled

blocks.text: A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.
Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but superior court judge William Sullivan set the retrial for 29 March in Plymouth superior court.

The decision to schedule Clancy’s second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court at 9am on 30 December to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is set for 18 February.
Clancy’s lawyers had argued that the judge should have investigated or removed the lone juror who opposed acquittal before declaring a mistrial.

A former labor and delivery nurse, Clancy has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time.
Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

articles.title: Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says
articles.summary:
Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the
articles.byline: Fiona Harvey, Graham Readfearn, Damien Gayle and Gabrielle Canon in Antalya

blocks.text: A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”

The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.

The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.

blocks.caption: The Cop31 negotiations president, Chris Bowen, speaking at a press conference after the launch of the draft text.  Photograph: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.

Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”

The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.

There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

He welcomed the fleshing out in the draft of a previous promise to triple finance to poor countries to help them adapt to the impacts of extreme weather. “If that language remains in the final version, it would suggest countries are starting to listen to the needs of the vulnerable,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

The “cover decision” is one part of the expected outcome of this Cop, and some countries – chiefly Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Arab group and some allies – have objected to having one. Cover decisions have been used in most of the 30 previous Cops, taking in resolutions that were difficult to fit into the other formal negotiating strands.
Within the other strands at Cop31, there are still major disagreements among developed and developing countries. Poor nations are unhappy that no new finance is likely to be forthcoming at this Cop.

“Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Mvundla of groundWork, an environmental justice nonprofit in South Africa. “The global south is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”

blocks.caption: Participants at Cop31. Photograph: Beyza Comert/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The text contains items likely to be subject to trade-offs among parties. For instance, language calling for “carbon dioxide removal” was attacked by campaigners who see it as a “false solution”, but it is unlikely that some fossil fuel-producing countries would agree any text without such a reference.

Bowen also said fossil fuel-producing countries did not bear more responsibility than consumer countries in tackling the climate crisis. “There are two types of countries in the world, fossil fuel exporters and fossil fuel importers, and we’re all in it together. The idea that everything [is for] fossil fuel exporters is not one I support,” he said. “We’re all part of this process, and just dealing with one and not the other is not realistic.”

He refused to commit Australia, which is one of the world’s biggest producers of coal, to a phaseout of fossil fuel exports, as campaigners and some countries are calling for, but said Australia had a plan to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions and was adjusting for a world in which all countries did the same.

“I accept the logic that all countries will need to reduce emissions, and that means they’re reducing their use of fossil fuels, and that will impact on Australia’s exports, absolutely,” he said. “That’s why we’re preparing our economy for that change.”

articles.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’

Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, as he joined Silicon Valley heavyweights in demanding the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.
The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia.
“He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return,” Trump said.

Trump’s comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that are in turn supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang, who resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Days before, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.
The letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged spy and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”.

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option.
“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.
after newsletter promotion
Meanwhile, the US government has also introduced new restrictions on chip sales designed to stop the technology being diverted to countries such as China.

The new rule announced on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Commerce Department said.

Huang reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy who also worked as an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed. Megaspeed is under suspicion, according to reports, of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Ms Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complies “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.
Nvidia shares opened down 2.7% on Monday, knocking about $100bn (£75.8bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82tn.

articles.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
articles.summary: In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson will be the new James BondImage: Amazon MGM Studios

blocks.text: After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.
How it all started
The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.
Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

blocks.caption: Bond girls were typically portrayed as ditzy blondes with little to sayImage: IFTN/United Archives/IMAGO

blocks.text: A machismo problem
Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.
Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.
In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.
Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

blocks.caption: The first bond girl was named Honey Ryder, a name which would likely be considered sexist by today's standardsImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Questionable lifestyle choices

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

blocks.caption: Even such artwork associated with the original Bond film would never be deemed appropriate in this day and ageImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why are all secretaries women?
In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.
Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.
Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.
In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

blocks.caption: It wasn't until the 2012 film that we finally learn something about Bond's boss's secretary, MoneypennyImage: CAP/MFS Image/Capital Pictures/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inappropriate casting

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.
If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

blocks.caption: White actor Joseph Wiseman was made to look Asian with makeupImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pattinson as a modern 007?

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.
Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.
This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

articles.title: Marcos emphasizes kapwa and interconnectivity at ASEAN Dinner
articles.summary: President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos hosted leaders of ASEAN member-nations and external partners around a Filipino table on Monday evening.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 12:43am
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. and First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos hosted leaders of ASEAN member-nations and external partners around a Filipino table on Monday evening.

"The strength of ASEAN goes beyond agendas and agreements. It is sustained by relationships, mutual trust, and the recognition that the peace, prosperity, and well-being of its Member States are interconnected," the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said.

President Marcos and the First Lady welcomed the guests to the Gala Dinner, "where the President highlighted kapwa, a Filipino value that embodies seeing ourselves in others and recognizing our shared identity, common humanity, and interconnected lives."

President Marcos also recalled that the regional bloc, for 60 years, worked on "building consultation, cooperation, and trust, emphasizing that its strength comes from generations of leaders and partners who have worked together for regional peace, prosperity, and resilience."
The PCO said the evening provided an opportunity for leaders to enjoy Filipino food, music, and hospitality. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Nvidia scandal: China's chips dilemma, US rivalry shape AI race
articles.summary: The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.

image.caption: The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industriesImage: Kobe Li/ZUMAPRESS/picture alliance

blocks.text: China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.
The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.
But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.
US moves to restrict China's access to chips
As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.
Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."
US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.

blocks.caption: Jensen Huang has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trump during his second termImage: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

blocks.text: Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week, enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.
Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trumpduring his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.
In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.
Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series, it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.

Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.
Nvidia affair and espionage allegations
But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.
How AI is changing the working world
The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.

Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.
China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.
Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.
"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.
It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."
Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.

A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"
Behind the verbal sparring lies an economic calculation.
Anthropic's market debut: Who'll win the race for AI?
Is China buying more US chips?

Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.
Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.
The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.

For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."
Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.
"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.

This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.

According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.
China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.
"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.
Will AI-powered autonomous weapons obey the laws of war?
China lacks advanced chip-making equipment
However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.
Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.
Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.

The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."

According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."

Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Tesla planning €3BN investment in German factory to produce Cybercabs
articles.summary: The Elon Musk-owned company is looking to further expand its only European production line. Brandenburg's state leader has welcomed the decision.

image.caption: Only a few places allow the driverless Cybercabs, including Austin, Texas, as seen hereImage: Bob Daemmrich/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The electric car manufacturer Tesla said on Monday it was planning to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in its German factory near Berlin so that it can start producing Cybercabs.

The plan to start production on the driverless taxis in Tesla's only European factory comes after billionaire owner Elon Musk announced last week that the company was shutting down Cybertruck production.
What do we know about Tesla's German factory expansion plan?
Construction work at the Grünheide complex is set to begin in 2027, with the first vehicles coming off the production line in 2029, according to company plans.
Capacity is set to reach 1 million units, according to the company, although it was unclear what timeframe this was in relation to.

Employment at the so-called "gigafactory" in the state of Brandenburg had dipped to around 11,000 before rising to 12,600 in October. The new expansion was expected to lead to the hiring of several hundred additional staff.
"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.
The company said it would submit an application for the new building by the end of the year.
German residents near Berlin fight for their drinking water
Brandenburg state premier says Tesla plans are a 'strong message'
Brandenburg's State Premier Dietmar Woidke welcomed the decision to expand the factory in his state.
"The €3 billion investment, and the prospect of producing up to a million Cybercabs in Grünheide in the future, is an enormously important economic decision," Woidke said in a statement.

"Especially in economically challenging times, this sends a strong message: Germany, even today, remains an attractive location for major industrial investments, and Brandenburg is showing how it's done," he added.
After a slump in sales put the expansion plans on hold, an uptick in demand he seen Tesla's fortunes back on the up.
It recently said it aims to increase weekly vehicle production to 7,500 units, equivalent to 375,000 a year. It also wants to expand its battery cell production on site.

blocks.caption: The Grünheide factory has sparked tensions with people living nearby over water accessImage: Jochen Eckel/picture alliance

articles.title: The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: how close are the connections?
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

image.caption: The new AfD youth wing 'Generation Germany' was set up in 2025Image: Marcus Golejewski/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, she has set herself an ambitious goal: together with her co-chair Alice Weidel, she aims to see Germany's next chancellor come from their party.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
The normalization of right-wing extremism?

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."
The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.
Young, far-right and radical? Meet the AfD's future leaders
Controversial distancing efforts within the AfD

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."
Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.
* Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
articles.summary:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore…

blocks.text: Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

blocks.caption: Hope Hostel in Kigali was prepared to house asylum seekers sent from Britain to Rwanda under the Conservatives’ prepared scheme.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

blocks.caption: The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the return hubs offered ‘a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe’.  Photograph: Radek Miča/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

articles.title: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
articles.summary: Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.

image.caption: Few Iranian families have not been touched by emigration or plans to leave IranImage: Egmont Strigl/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.
Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.
"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.
"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?

She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.
Turkey as a stopover

"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."
Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.
Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

A US naval blockade of Iranian ports ⁠in ⁠the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.
The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.
The hopes and fears of Iranians in Germany
She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."
Young Iranians lose faith in the future

The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.
A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.
The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.
Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.
Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.
"That's my dream of a better future," he said.
Fleeing Iran for freedom
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds
articles.summary:
‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows

The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler”

blocks.text: The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.
In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.

Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.

“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”

Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.

More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found. The growth of AI is being underpinned by a rise in new gas-fired power, sometimes built at the site of the facilities themselves, which is being favored over installed renewables such as solar and wind.

“Sadly, it doesn’t surprise me that the majority of hyperscale datacenters rely on fossil fuels for their power generation despite the profound and lasting climate and health impacts that could be, and should be, avoided,” said Gina McCarthy, a former climate adviser to Joe Biden’s administration who said that the study is an “important step” to assessing the impact of datacenters.

The rise of datacenters has caused alarm among climate groups amid worsening global heating that may surpass previously agreed “safe” levels and cause an acceleration of the sort of deadly events seen this year, such roasting heatwaves in Europe, wildfire smoke in North America and the disastrous landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border.

In the US, the epicenter of this AI boom, developers have defended the use of energy and water used by the facilities as marginal when compared with other industries, such as agriculture, and have touted associated jobs and raised local taxes as beneficial for communities. Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the AI industry, has said people who oppose the growth of datacenters will end up “backwards and poor”.

But a bipartisan public backlash to datacenters shows little sign of abating in the US. Local opposition has focused on several big developments, such as a cluster of datacenters in the greater Memphis, Tennessee, region that are central to Elon Musk’s AI ambitions but have faced protests and lawsuits over their noise and air pollution. Musk’s AI company has responded to this by buying the homes of those who live nearby.

The vast water use of one of the world’s largest planned datacenters in drought-hit Utah, meanwhile, has mobilized grassroots opprobrium. The site, called Stratos, will also emit a large amount of air pollution, a separate study recently found.

Stratos could cause health-related economic costs of up to $690m each year if it uses the dirtiest of the fossil fuel options to power itself, this research concluded. Burning this fuel will release up to 3,140 tons of soot-like particulate matter, linked to an array of cardiovascular and respiratory problems in people, in plumes that will waft across Utah and into Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and Illinois.

“Stratos is a modern-day Trojan horse that would unleash deadly air pollution linked to serious, life-threatening health damages upon Utah communities and millions of people living downwind of this massive datacenter,” said John Walke, director of federal clean air at the Natural Resources Defense Council, which commissioned the report.
“Pollution from Stratos will contaminate the air and compromise the ability to live a healthy life both around the facility and in states hundreds of miles from the datacenter.”

The developers for the Stratos project have been planning to use combined-cycle natural gas but are also reportedly considering using renewables and other options; they have been under political pressure to reduce its scale. Last month the project filed a new water application that reportedly claimed its water demands would be lower than historical agricultural uses at the property, which some environmental critics have questioned.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Toronto police say one man has been arrested in last month's violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood.
Man, 23, is same suspect police say was treated for gunshot wound and released from hospital prior to arrest
The 23-year-old man is the same suspect who police say was treated for a gunshot wound and released from hospital before investigators had the evidence to arrest him.

articles.title: Philippines, Japan vow to deepen strategic partnership
articles.summary: President Marcos met with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi yesterday on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits where they reaffirmed their…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi hold bilateral talks at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City on November 16, 2026
PPA Pool photos by Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos met with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi yesterday on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits where they reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthen the two countries’ strategic partnership.
Takaichi met with Marcos at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, hours after arriving in Manila.
During the meeting, Marcos thanked the Japanese leader for participating in the ASEAN Summit here.
“I remember with great pleasure our karaoke session…over dinner in our last meeting,” Marcos told Takaichi, drawing laughter from Philippine and Japanese officials in attendance.
Marcos also cited significant progress in advancing relations between Manila and Tokyo.
Takaichi, for her part, said she is looking forward to further deepening ties with Manila.

“Based on our comprehensive strategic partnership between Japan and the Philippines, I look forward to further strengthening our bilateral relations through our meeting after this,” she said, as translated in English.
Takaichi will participate in the ASEAN Summit as dialogue partner of the regional bloc.
She will also co-chair the 4th Asia Zero Emission Community Leaders’ Meeting scheduled tomorrow.
AZEC is a Japan-led initiative aimed at promoting clean energy, reducing carbon emissions and supporting sustainable economic growth while strengthening energy security across the region.
The two leaders met in May during Marcos’ state visit to Japan, when the two countries elevated their relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

In October, the two leaders also held a telephone conversation, where they discussed various areas of cooperation, such as on the Luzon Economic Corridor, defense and security and Japan’s long-standing support to peace consolidation efforts in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region of Muslim Mindanao.

articles.title: Government seeks to reduce US tariff during Trump visit
articles.summary: The Philippines wants to see a reduction in the 12.5 percent tariff being imposed on its exports to the United States when President Marcos and US President Donald Trump meet in Manila this week.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Youth groups join the ‘Kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio’ of different indigenous groups in Manila on November 16, 2026, to protest US President Donald Trump’s visit.
Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines wants to see a reduction in the 12.5 percent tariff being imposed on its exports to the United States when President Marcos and US President Donald Trump meet in Manila this week.

At a press conference yesterday following the conclusion of the 28th Association of the Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Economic Community Council gathering, Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said the 12.5 percent tariff imposed by the US on Philippine exports would be among the topics to be discussed during the bilateral meeting between Marcos and Trump.
“Of course my wish is to bring down the tariff,” she said. “That’s really what [we want] because we want to be able to expand the exports to the US and to all other markets globally.”
Last July, the US imposed a 12.5 percent tariff on goods from the Philippines and other economies to make up for gaps in prohibiting imports produced with forced labor.
The 12.5 percent tariff replaced the 10 percent levy earlier slapped on Philippine exports to the US after the US Supreme Court declared as unconstitutional the reciprocal tariffs imposed last year.
In July, the trade, finance and labor departments signed a joint administrative order (JAO) establishing a mechanism for investigating and blocking imports produced through forced labor.

Under the JAO, an inter-agency committee was created to evaluate and conduct a probe on complaints on imports suspected to have been produced through forced labor. Roque said the US has received a copy of the JAO.
“We will be discussing actually on Nov. 18 all of this,” she said.
Earlier, Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo said he is “reasonably optimistic” that the JAO to prohibit imports made through forced labor would help lift the 12.5 percent tariff.
The US is the top destination for Philippine merchandise exports, accounting for $13.46 billion or 15.9 percent of the country’s exports last year.
From January to September, the US remained the leading market for Philippine exports of goods with a 20.2 percent share valued at $14.95 billion.

articles.title: SC: Seafarers’ bond for seeking damages unconstitutional
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has rendered unconstitutional a bond requirement for seafarers seeking to execute monetary awards and damages under Republic Act 12021 or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Aspiring seafarers gather at the ‘Seafarer’s Tambayan’ along T.M. Kalaw Avenue in Manila in March this year, hoping to secure placements on cargo ships.
Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has rendered unconstitutional a bond requirement for seafarers seeking to execute monetary awards and damages under Republic Act 12021 or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.
Under Section 59 of the said law, seafarers seeking to execute monetary awards and damages should post a bond “to ensure restitution should the award be subsequently reversed or modified.”

However, the SC said the bond requirement “violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution (as it) imposed a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments and subjected them to a disadvantage not similarly imposed on other workers.”

It also voided related orders from the Department of Labor and Employment that enforced the bond requirement, and from the Department of Migrant Workers on the use of its Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan fund to pay bond premiums.

At the same time, Section 1, Rule XXII of the implementing rules and regulations of RA 12021 was “declared ultra vires and void” for “contravening” another provision in the law that “preserves the rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers before its effectivity.”

Also declared unconstitutional was Section 60 of the same law and Section 4 of RA 10706 or the Seafarers Protection Act, which both imposed rules on how lawyers should represent seafarers in related cases, including “a 10 percent ceiling on fees, requirements for notarized certifications and undertakings and rules governing the collection of fees from seafarers.”

“While Congress may enact measures to protect seafarers against ambulance chasing and abusive practices, the regulation of lawyers’ professional conduct and the practice of law remains within the Supreme Court’s exclusive authority,” it maintained.

On the other hand, the high court upheld the constitutionality of other provisions in the Magna Carta on maritime education and training. It declared that under the said law, the Maritime Industry Authority was authorized to impose “standards intended to ensure the quality of maritime education, the competency of Filipino seafarers and compliance with applicable international maritime standards.”

“Particularly, the requirements relating to enrollment and available shipboard training opportunities were considered reasonable measures to address the availability of practical training for maritime students. The prohibition against charging tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third-party providers was likewise sustained as a measure against unjustified charges,” the SC noted.

The decision penned by SC Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh resolved the five consolidated petitions raised by seafarers, labor organizations and maritime educational institutions against the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers.

articles.title: Political will, partnerships needed to achieve SDGs
articles.summary: With only less than half of the Sustainable Development Goals progressing as planned, President Marcos yesterday called for political will and enhanced partnerships to meet the targets requiring…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on November 16, 2026
PPA Pool photos by Mike Alquinto

MANILA, Philippines — With only less than half of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) progressing as planned, President Marcos yesterday called for political will and enhanced partnerships to meet the targets requiring global action on poverty, inequality and other problems.

In remarks delivered during the 16th Association of Southeast Asian Nations-United Nations (ASEAN-UN) Summit yesterday, Marcos noted that 2030 is less than four years away, but only 36 percent of accessible SDG targets are on track.

“Achieving these goals requires renewed political will, stronger partnerships with the private sector and cooperation that is evidence-based and responsive to the needs of its members, especially developing countries,” Marcos said.
The SDGs are 17 targets calling for a global effort to end poverty and to carry out strategies on improving health and education, reducing inequality and promoting economic growth.
It is in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development adopted by all UN member-states in 2015.

The goals include end poverty in all its forms everywhere; end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture; ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages; ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all; achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls; ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all; ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all; promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all; build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation.

The other SDGs are reduce inequality within and among countries; make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable; ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns; take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts; conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development; protect, restore and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification and halt and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss; promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development; provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels; strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the Global Partnership for Sustainable Development.

In a statement, the Presidential Communications Office said ASEAN and UN leaders had reaffirmed cooperation under their Plan of Action for 2026-2030, which covers peace and security, digital transformation, climate action, disaster management, health and the protection of women and children.

MANILA, Philippines — Around 600,000 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) across Southeast Asia stand to benefit from the adoption by ASEAN leaders of the Philippine-spearheaded “ASEAN Declaration on Fair, Ethical and Sustainable Recruitment for Empowered Migrant Workers.”

“This Declaration advances ASEAN instruments toward the protection and promotion of rights of migrant workers. With this Declaration, there will be greater transparency and accountability in recruitment and placement across all ASEAN member-states – prohibiting excessive or unreasonable recruitment fees, strengthening agency licensing and monitoring and promoting access to justice and complaint mechanisms,” DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said.

articles.title: Calibrated restoration eyed for Myanmar representation
articles.summary: Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations have decided to pursue a calibrated engagement, step-by-step and progress-based approach to restore Myanmar’s political representation.

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro answers questions from the media during a press briefing at the International Media Center in Pasay City on November 16, 2026
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations have decided to pursue a calibrated engagement, step-by-step and progress-based approach to restore Myanmar’s political representation.
Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said the ASEAN leaders adopted on Sunday a decision and review on the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus (5PC).
“The foreign ministers will continue the constructive and principled engagement with Myanmar in accordance with the Five-Point Consensus,” Lazaro said.
The leaders expressed deep concern over the conflicts and humanitarian situation in Myanmar, and took note of the recommendations during the ASEAN foreign ministers’ meetings on July 21 and Nov. 14.

“We underscored the need for ASEAN to calibrate its engagement with Myanmar based on developments on the ground, in a manner that encourages further progress in the implementation of the 5PC,” they said.

The leaders denounced the acts of violence in Myanmar against civilians and public facilities, and urged all parties involved to take concrete action to immediately halt indiscriminate violence, denounce any escalation, exercise utmost restraint, ensure the protection and safety of all civilians and civilian infrastructure.

They urged all parties to create a conducive environment for the delivery of humanitarian assistance to the people in need in Myanmar and a national political dialogue. They also appreciated the efforts to ensure progress on the implementation of the 5PC in its entirety, with the sole objective of restoring peace, stability and democracy through a Myanmar-owned and -led approach.

“We commended the work of the ASEAN chair, through its Special Envoy (Lazaro), in establishing inclusive engagements with all relevant stakeholders in Myanmar by promoting national inclusive dialogue, reaching out to parties concerned, including regional and international organizations, in a sustainable manner, towards reaching a Myanmar-owned and -led resolution to the situation in Myanmar,” the statement read.

articles.title: TikTok, DOT launch interactive virtual heritage site tours

AFP / Kirill Kudryavtsev
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Tourism has tapped social media platform TikTok to promote UNESCO-recognized heritage sites in the country through immersive livestreaming tours.
The live tour generated nearly six million impressions, with 73,000 viewers from Southeast Asia, the United Kingdom and Australia, according to TikTok.
The program also features real-time conversations, allowing viewers to interact with the virtual tour by asking questions.

“TikTok is a really good platform for us to start talking and start learning about heritage. Content creators have the ability to start these conversations. It doesn’t have to be too academic or technical,” said Ivan Anthony Henares, secretary-general of the UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines.

“Beyond entertainment, we want to see more content creators use their talents to bring heritage to life, share their personal stories and create educational content that inspires meaningful engagement,” said Chin Zhao Wei, TikTok LIVE brand and reputation manager.
The collaboration aims to create more opportunities for cultural institutions, experts and creators to share Philippine heritage with wider audiences through responsible storytelling.

articles.title: Philippines, Australia reaffirm defense ties
articles.summary: The Philippines and Australia yesterday reaffirmed their defense ties as they expressed “concern over what they described as “coercive, aggressive and dangerous” against Filipino…

blocks.text: November 17, 2026 | 12:00am

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (L) walks out with Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. after his address to the House of Representatives at the Parliament House in Canberra on February 29, 2024. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos told Australia's parliament on February 29 that his country was on the "frontline" of a battle against powers undermining regional peace, but would not capitulate in maritime disputes with the likes of China.
AFP / David Gray

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Australia yesterday reaffirmed their defense ties as they expressed “concern over what they described as “coercive, aggressive and dangerous” against Filipino ships in the South China Sea.

In a joint statement released after a bilateral meeting between President Marcos and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, the two countries vowed to deepen their political and strategic cooperation and strengthen engagement between their officials and armed forces.

“The Philippines and Australia reaffirm our Strategic Partnership, established in 2023 and underpinned by longstanding cooperation, shared democratic values and a common vision for a peaceful, stable and prosperous region where strategic agency is freely exercised and sovereignty is upheld,” the statement read.

“As we commemorate the 80th year of the establishment of our diplomatic relations this year, and at a time of rising uncertainties, we commit to expand our bilateral security and defense relations,” it added. The two countries also reiterated the importance of peace and stability in the maritime domain.

“We remain seriously concerned about the situation in the South China Sea, particularly the coercive, aggressive, and dangerous actions against Filipino nationals and vessels. In the tenth anniversary year of the South China Sea Arbitral Tribunal Award of 12 July 2016, we reaffirm the final and binding nature of the Award on the parties to the Arbitration,” they said.

The Philippines and Australia also committed to “expand cooperation and act in support of maritime safety and security, freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the seas in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.”
Also during the ASEAN-Australia Summit, Albanese announced a new digital cooperation package designed to deepen Australia’s partnership with the regional bloc.

“It will accelerate ASEAN’s digital transformation and boost economic growth by strengthening the region’s digital ecosystem, supporting AI safety standards and building a digital workforce,” Albanese said.
