articles.title: Silicon Valley leaders call for reinstatement of Nvidia CEO with 'Stand With Jensen' petition
articles.summary: A petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is drawing support from prominent Silicon Valley personalities, four days after his resignation stemming from revelations of multiple…

image.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks after attending the AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo, on July 16. (Manami Yamada/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

A petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is drawing support from prominent Silicon Valley personalities, four days after his resignation stemming from revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy.
Signatories include Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney

More than 179,000 people had signed the petition, according to the website hosting it. Those listed as signatories included Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.
Nvidia shares suffered early losses, but remained more than one per cent lower after U.S. President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang return as CEO.
"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said.

The Stand With Jensen website coincided with an open letter from two prominent investors, Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, who urged Nvidia's board to avoid rushing to replace Huang before all the facts were known.

"We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," according to an open letter published on the website.

The website showed that more than 8,400 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees, claiming this represents approximately 21 per cent of all Nvidia employees. A further 94,000 signatories identified themselves as shareholders, although the website cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified.
Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO

The campaign comes as some prominent investors also urge Nvidia's board not to rush to replace Huang. Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that the board should wait until all the facts were known.
Shockwaves through industry

Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.

Corporate boards have previously removed chief executives over relationships with employees. McDonald's fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy, while Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 after a similar policy breach.

items: Huang resigns after affair raises national security concerns
Espionage, chips and the 'Nvidia state'
Could Nvidia survive without its ultra-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang?

blocks.text: But the episode also highlights the challenges boards can face when ousting high-profile executives who retain strong employee and investor backing. OpenAI reinstated Sam Altman as CEO in November 2023, just days after his removal triggered an employee revolt and opposition from investors.
The turmoil at Nvidia comes as the company is taking on growing strategic importance in Washington.
Is the Nvidia scandal fracturing Trump's administration?

Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $13 million US and $62 million US in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.
The Trump administration also plans to designate Nvidia and more than two dozen other AI companies as "national champions," the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to appoint an outsider as its next CEO, saying the company needs a "dramatic shakeup" following Huang's departure.
Colette Kress was named interim CEO in the wake of Huang’s resignation. She previously served as executive vice-president and chief financial officer.
The website hosting the petition included a call to institutional investors to dial into an earnings call slated for Tuesday and raise the issue of Huang’s ousting.
U.S. President Donald Trump stands with Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington on Oct. 8. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

blocks.text: The two P-pop groups are nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category
MANILA, Philippines – History is made as P-pop groups SB19 and BINI are nominated for the 69th Grammy Awards.
The Recording Academy announced on Monday, November 16 (Manila time), that the two Filipino music acts were nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category.
SB19 received a nomination for the song “VISA,” while BINI was nominated for “Unang Kilig.”
“From the Philippines to the world, thank you for believing in SB19 and standing with us as we carry Filipino music to the global stage!” SB19 said about its nomination.

“A historic moment for OPM, for Filipino music, and for everyone who believes in them. The girls are making history, and we couldn’t be prouder! Thank you to everyone who continues to support us!” BINI wrote.

Under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, SB19 and BINI are joined by fellow nominees, K-pop girl groups IVE (“BANG BANG”) and KiiiKiii (“404 (New Era)”), Japanese soloist LiSA (“Yes”), and Japanese kawaii metal band BABYMETAL and American rock outfit Polyphia (“Sunset Kiss”).
SB19 and BINI’s nominations come at a time when the two groups have achieved several major milestones all year.

BINI became the first-ever homegrown Filipino music act to perform at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in April, while SB19 later achieved the same feat in July at Lollapalooza in Chicago.
SB19 will also be heading to Coachella in April 2027. Their inclusion in the lineup was just announced on November 11.
BINI, meanwhile, just wrapped up their 2026 BINI Signals World Tour in Taiwan on November 15. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem to step down in 2027
articles.summary: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term leading Canada's central bank. His current term as governor will end on June 2, 2027.

image.caption: Tiff Macklem, the governor of the Bank of Canada, will leave his post in 2027. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term leading Canada's central bank. His current term as governor will end on June 2, 2027.
Central bank says it has started search for Macklem's successor
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will step down from the top job at Canada's central bank when his term expires on June 2, 2027.

In an announcement on Monday, the Bank of Canada said Macklem will not seek a second term as governor when his current seven-year term expires in June. The central bank says it has begun its search for his successor.
"My time as governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world," Macklem, 65, stated on Monday.
"The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate."
Mackelm's retirement was widely expected, as the last time a ​Bank of Canada governor served a second term was ​1980.
During his tenure, Macklem faced unprecedented challenges, including the inflation shock resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, and the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.
More to follow

Two men have been charged following an incident in Birmingham, where a man was…

blocks.text: Two men have been charged following an incident in Birmingham, where a man was run over by a van after flags were removed from lamp-posts.
A man in his 30s was taken to hospital with leg injuries after the incident on Mayfield Road in the suburb of Stirchley, south-west Birmingham, on 14 May.
Mark Keating, 49, from Tamworth, has been charged with four counts of assault by beating and will appear before magistrates in Birmingham on 9 December, West Midlands police said on Monday.

Ryan Bridge, 45, from Bromsgrove, is charged with two counts of using threatening/abusive words/behaviour likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress. He will appear before the same court on 10 December.
Another man, 53, from Sutton Coldfield, remains on bail after being arrested on suspicion of wounding in May.
In a statement, West Midlands police said the van was recovered nearby, shortly after the incident.

“Officers have been carrying out a range of thorough enquiries to establish the full circumstances around what happened,” the statement read. “We took reports of four assaults relating to the same incident, but we understand that no one suffered serious injuries.”

articles.title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
articles.summary: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.

blocks.text: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title: Mamdani disbands controversial NYPD unit accused of using excessive force
articles.summary:
Mayor axes strategic response group that cracked down on protesters and announces new community safety division

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced Monday that he was disbanding…

blocks.text: Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years from civil rights groups who have accused the unit of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters.

In a video released Monday morning, Mamdani said the move stemmed from a campaign pledge he made to disband the New York City police department’s strategic response group (SRG). “Today, we are keeping that promise,” Mamdani said in the video.

An accompanying joint statement from Mamdani and NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch said the overhaul would “transform how the city prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest”.

Along with eliminating the SRG, which was founded in 2015 ostensibly to focus on counter-terrorism, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement also said that the city planned to establish a “first-of-its-kind, civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD)” within the mayor’s office of community safety.
That division will not have weapons or arrest powers, unlike the SRG, according to the announcement.

The city will also establish what they described as a “specialized dialogue team” that will be known as the “First Amendment Support Team” (Fast) within the NYPD’s community affairs bureau, Mamdani and Tisch’s statement said. The creation of Fast is meant to “improve the NYPD’s protest response,” and it will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation, the mayor and police commissioner said.
Additionally, their statement said, the NYPD will create a new patrol support division (PSD) within its patrol services bureau.
Plans call for the unit to be staffed with vetted officers who will primarily perform patrol-related duties and receive specialized crowd management training to support responses to demonstrations.

The reforms also introduce “significant new restrictions on the tactics and weapons” officers can use during protests and demonstrations – banning irritant gas, kettling and long guns. Responding officers will no longer be allowed to deploy pepper spray “as a crowd-management tool” – and “long-range acoustic devices” meant to affect protesters’ hearing “will be limited to 90 decibels,” Mamdani and Tisch said in their statement.

Under the new structure, the mayor said, the SRG’s counter-terrorism functions – “including heavy weapons deployments at critical infrastructure” – will be consolidated within the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau.

The statement said that helped ensure a complete separation between the city’s counter-terrorism operations and protests protected by the rights to free speech and assembly guaranteed by the US constitution’s first amendment.

Tisch said that the new structure was “designed to consolidate our counterterrorism capabilities, provide greater support to our patrol officers and ensure we continue to respond to protests consistent with public safety and the first amendment”.
“These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department” she said.
The administration said that the SRG-related reforms come at “no additional cost and without increasing or reducing NYPD headcount”.
While civil rights groups hailed Monday’s announcement, the New York Police Benevolent Association’s president, Patrick Hendry, criticized it in a statement on social media.

“Today is not a good day for New Yorkers who just want a safe and orderly city,” said the statement from Hendry, whose organization is a labor union representing more than 21,000 active NYPD officers. “Mayor Mamdani is showing his true colors: he’s willing to put your safety and police officers’ safety at risk to appease his radical base.
“So the next time your life is disrupted by demonstrators who are blocking bridges and roadways or causing chaos on our streets, remember: Mayor Mamdani is on their side, not yours.”

Mamdani in January had reiterated promises to disband the SRG after it arrested dozens of demonstrators occupying a hotel lobby in protests opposing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency at the forefront of the mass deportation campaign which Donald Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

Furthermore, after 2020 protests over a Minneapolis police officer’s murder of George Floyd, New York City’s department of investigation recommended that the NYPD “reevaluate the central role” of the SRG “in response to large protests given their orientation to handle counterterrorism, riots, and other serious threats, and better calibrate their use to circumstances that require such specialized force”.

articles.title: William and Kate in India for 1st overseas trip together since her cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

image.caption: Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, board a metro train in Mumbai, India, on Monday. (Rafiq Maqbool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Photos
Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
3-day trip marks significant return to overseas royal engagements for Princess of Wales
Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, their first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. William, who, like his father, King Charles, has made campaigning on the environment one ⁠of his biggest causes, founded the ⁠Earthshot Prize in 2020 with the aim of finding solutions to climate change. It awards each of the five winners $1.86 million Cdn.

items: Facing 'uncomfortable' questions, King Charles shows the 'soft power' of the Crown
Prince Harry says he wants to reconcile with the Royal Family. It may not be so easy

blocks.text: The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established, will feature several prominent guests, including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, making its debut performance in India.
"India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country," William posted on social media.

Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighbourhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.
Kate plays a game of street cricket in Mumbai on Monday. (Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty Images)
Kate plays cricket in Ballard Estate. (Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters)
Kate laughing. (Rafiq Maqbool/The Associated Press)

The couple will also attend events highlighting India's cricket, fashion and film industries before travelling to New Delhi, where they are scheduled to meet with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India a decade ago, before William became the heir to the U.K. throne.

The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery.
Kate, 44, disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
William and Kate meet locals in Mumbai on Monday. (Ian Vogler/Getty Images)
Her treatment included preventative chemotherapy and she says the illness still impacts ​her life.

Since her illness, Kate has significantly reduced her official workload, saying ⁠she is taking each day as it ​comes. While her public appearances have gradually increased, she has not joined William on previous foreign trips.
Her only significant overseas visit since 2024 came in May when she travelled alone to Italy for two days as part of her work focusing on early childhood development.

"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time," she said in an interview published this week in Country Life magazine, for which William was guest editor.
Kate in Mumbai on Monday. (Punit Paranjpe/AFP/Getty Images)
With files from Reuters

articles.title: N.L. families to receive $500 per child before the end of the year
articles.summary: Families in Newfoundland and Labrador who receive the Canada Child Benefit will receive $500 per child under the age of 18 as part of the province’s latest affordability measure connected to…

image.caption: N.L. Finance Minister Craig Pardy and Premier Tony Wakeham announced families will recieve $500 per child in the province's latest affordability benefit. (Terry Roberts/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

Families in Newfoundland and Labrador who receive the Canada Child Benefit will receive $500 per child under the age of 18 as part of the province’s latest affordability measure connected to skyrocketing oil revenues.
Announcement is province's latest affordability measure connected to high oil revenues

Families in Newfoundland and Labrador who receive the Canada Child Benefit will get a one-time $500 payment per child as part of the province’s latest affordability measure connected to skyrocketing oil revenues.
At an announcement Monday morning, Premier Tony Wakeham said families will receive a tax-free payment for children under the age of 18.
The top-up will cost the province $36 million, and Wakeham said it will help about 46,500 families and 77,000 children across the province.
“That is money back in people's pockets,” said Wakeham.

For families where the parents aren’t in the same household, Finance Minister Craig Pardy said the funds will go to whichever parent is receiving the Canada Child Benefit. He also said parents will receive it by the end of the year.
Pardy said the amount was determined by looking at projected oil revenues.
The government has announced other affordability measures in the last few months, including $100 to $500 payments to seniors making $100,000 or less annually.

In September, Pardy announced high oil prices have boosted Newfoundland and Labrador’s revenue, and that 80 per cent of the extra revenues will be used against the province’s debt, while 20 percent will be used for affordability measures.
Pardy told reporters that as long as the province continues to collect the higher than usual oil revenues, people can expect more affordability measure announcements.
“I think we'll respond to affordability as best we [can] and I can probably envision another,” he said.

articles.title: Philippines eyes more Filipino products in South Korea amid trade talks
articles.summary: The Philippines is eyeing more opportunities for Filipino exporters to sell their products in South Korea amid ongoing discussions to upgrade the free trade agreement between the Association of…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 10:50pm

The Philippines is eyeing more opportunities for Filipino exporters to sell their products in South Korea amid ongoing discussions to upgrade the free trade agreement between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and Seoul.

During the 27th ASEAN–Republic of Korea Summit chaired by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Monday, both sides aim to achieve a substantial conclusion of their upgraded free trade pact by the end of 2027 to help expand market access across the region.

In his speech, Marcos underscored the more than three decades of relations between the regional bloc and South Korea, noting that the nations are pursuing greater opportunities for regional cooperation across various fields through the Plan of Action 2026 to 2030.

“Over three decades, our relations have evolved into a comprehensive strategic partnership grounded in mutual trust, shared interest, and a common vision for peace, stability, and prosperity. Our cooperation is now guided by the ASEAN-Republic of Korea Plan of Action 2026 to 2030,” Marcos said.

The Plan of Action outlines joint efforts to bolster maritime safety and energy security, leverage artificial intelligence for digital advancement, and deepen partnerships in healthcare as well as technical and vocational education and training.
Marcos also welcomed Seoul’s sustained backing of the bloc’s long-term goals and regional leadership.

“We welcome the Republic of Korea's continued support for ASEAN Community Vision 2045, ASEAN centrality, and ASEAN-led mechanisms. We look forward to strengthening our cooperation in upholding international law and advancing an open, inclusive, and peaceful region,” the President said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Raye, Rosalia and Dolly Parton recognised in Grammy nominations
articles.summary: British singer Raye lands 11 nominations while Dolly Parton is recognised two months after her death.

blocks.text: Raye, Rosalia and Dolly Parton recognised in Grammy nominations
Image source, Getty Images
Raye's latest record This Album May Contain Hope also won the Mercury Prize last month
BySteven McIntosh
Entertainment reporter
British singer Raye leads the charge at this year's Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with two posthumous nods.
Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.
Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.
Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.
Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.
The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.
That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.
Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.
Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rosalía's nominations comes after she won big at last weeks' Latin Grammy Awards

blocks.text: Rosalía's nominations comes after she won big at last weeks' Latin Grammy Awards
There are five new categories this year, including best Latin song and best Asian pop music performance.
They have been added as part of the Academy's attempts to make the event "more inclusive" and represent a wider range of music genres.

However, critics fear that the new specialist categories will result in genres such as K-pop being under-represented in the major categories, and acts including BTS and Stray Kids have said they will boycott this year's ceremony.
Instead, the nominees for the first Asian pop music performance included Babymetal and Lisa from Blackpink.
Songs and albums had to be released between 31 August 2025 and 28 August 2026 to qualify for this year's event.
Around 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy are eligible to vote for the winners.

articles.title: Guinea's gold rush: Arrests, deportations spark outcry
articles.summary: Guinea has banned illegal gold mining, citing environmental concerns. It has further charged hundreds of suspected local and foreign illegal miners amid reports of rights abuses and deportations.

image.caption: Guinea wants to start refining some of its gold locallyImage: A_STOCK1992/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: In Siguiri, northeastern Guinea, the gold rush has come to an abrupt end. "To date, 1,263 people, including Guineans, Burkinabe, Malians, Togolese, Nigerians, Ivorians, and Ghanaians, have been arrested and taken to Conakry for legal proceedings," Guinea's army spokesman, General Mamadou Aliou Sow, said. He added that officers from the Criminal Investigation Division, the National Police, and the National Gendarmerie are currently conducting interrogations.

The operation follows the ban on illegal gold mining in the Siguiri administrative region. According to Guinean authorities, the aim is to stop mining practices considered harmful to the environment. Uncontrolled gold mining depletes the soil, destroy vegetation and choke waterways.

blocks.caption: For many West Africans, including Guinea, artisanal mining is a key source of livelihood Image: Mike Goldwater/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We know that there have recently been various forms of gold mining here involving the use of chemicals that can destroy the environmentand pollute our water sources," Toumany Sangare, chairman of the Siguiri civil society council, told DW.

The closure of the mining sites is having a significant impact on the local economy. For many workers, it means the sudden loss of their main source of income. DW spoke with young gold panners from Burkina Faso who had been driven out of Siguiri. Some said they had walked more than 200 km (124 miles) to the Malian capital, Bamako.

"We tried our luck, but just as we were beginning to feel hopeful, we were told to leave," Noufa, in his early 20s, who arrived in Siguiri in early October to work in a small mine, told DW. Another Burkinabe, who goes by the name Mc One, told DW he set out for Siguiri to earn money to provide for his elderly parents and relatives. "I left just under five months ago. We went through very difficult times there."
Did Guinean authorities target foreigners?

Guinean authorities refute the allegation that the ban on gold mining specifically targeted foreigners, saying the measure applies to all illegal gold miners. The closure of the mine primarily affects Guineans, Mohamed Nabe, chairman of the Committee on Mining and Industry, told DW.

"Millions of Guineans are affected by this, compared to just a few thousand foreigners," Nabe said, adding that like everywhere else, there are cross-border population movements. "Of course, this can raise certain security concerns, but it was not the security aspect that motivated this decision. The main reasons are environmental in nature, as well as the need to better organize, structure, and regulate the mining sector."
The hidden cost of illegal gold mining in Ghana

Supporting the move, Morissanda Kouyate, Guinea's Foreign Minister, said his country is not the only one to ban illegal gold mining. However, according to Burkina Faso's Minister of Security, Mahamadou Sana, the deported nationals were allegedly subjected to "cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment." He spoke of "brutality" and alleged that the operation had resulted in deaths and injuries.

Malian journalist Amadou Oumar Diallo also criticized the alleged brutality of the Guinean authorities. In his view, they violated human rights. "Normally, when you prevent someone from exercising their freedom, you also have to provide for them," Diallo told DW. "This care is expensive. Detention alone costs a lot of money. The Guinean government took the easy way out by refusing to adhere to these principles and deporting all these people."

While Burkina Faso strongly condemned the treatment of gold panners, Mali's leadership initially adopted a somewhat more restrained tone. Officially, Bamako described Guinea's decision to expel the miners as "sovereign."

Most recently, however, Mali's Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maiga, spoke of a "humanitarian catastrophe." On November 8, he traveled to Kouremale on the border between Mali and Guinea, where dozens of deported Malians were returning to the country. Given the close ties between Mali and Guinea, Maiga regretted the lack of coordination between the two countries.

Currently, authorities in Mali and Burkina Faso are organizing efforts to assist their citizens: buses and trucks have been mobilized from both Bamako and Ouagadougou to bring the deported gold miners back to their home countries.
Guinea opens its first gold refinery

Parallel to the events in Siguiri, the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR) has begun operations in Conakry. With this, Guinea joins other West African nations such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and Cote d'Ivoire. The Guinean government's goal is to refine 30% of the 70 metric tons (70,000 kg) of gold mined in the country domestically.

Dr. Ibrahim Diallo, a mining expert, suggested that the Guinean authorities may have wanted to bring the gold mines in Siguiri under their control to supply the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR). "What's happening in Siguiri isn't gold panning. A gold panner doesn't use a bulldozer or an excavator."
Joining forces to protect Guinea's Tristao Islands

Patrick Schein, chairman of the Alliance for Responsible Mining (ARM), told DW that it made more sense for Guinea to build up reserves with domestic gold rather than imported gold. However, he also stressed that the gold must be certified to be internationally recognized.

He does not anticipate significant local demand, so exports are crucial. It remains to be seen whether the refinery in Conakry can be competitive in this regard. For jewelry manufacturing, for example, international-level technical expertise is required.

Another issue, according to the ARM chairman, is that the location of refining determines the gold's origin. "So if I'm in Guinea and import or buy gold that comes from another country, that gold becomes Guinean gold through local refining," Schein said. "If Guinea serves as a transit hub for gold from the subregion, it would—unintentionally—become a center for money laundering," he added.

According to Schein, tracing refined gold is harder than tracing raw gold. However, if the goal of refining [gold] in Guinea is to ensure better traceability, pay miners better wages and create a mercury-free processing chain, then that is a good initiative. "But now this must also be put into practice."
Mohamed Toure in Conakry and Mahamadou Kane in Bamako contributed to this article
This article was originally written in German

articles.title: Climate advocates at COP31 urge probe into mass arrests at ASEAN protests
articles.summary: Pax Silica, a key issue in the ASEAN protests, is opposed by many environmental and climate groups as well

blocks.text: PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump's visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Rappler
Pax Silica, a key issue in the ASEAN protests, is opposed by many environmental and climate groups as well

items: Filipino climate justice advocates at COP31 are demanding an independent investigation into the mass arrests of protesters during the ASEAN Summit in Manila.
The groups emphasize the connection between environmental issues and human rights, calling for accountability and the rejection of the Pax Silica initiative, which threatens indigenous rights.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino climate justice and environmental advocates present at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, are urging an independent probe into the mass arrests of people who joined the protests against the ASEAN Summit back in Manila.

“Whether at COP31 or the ASEAN Summit, the government cannot speak of a peoples-centered future while treating their voices as a security threat,” read the groups’ statement released Monday, November 16.
They demanded “an independent, transparent and immediate investigation into the arbitrary mass arrests and illegal detention.”
Climate justice activists underscored the link between the fight for the planet and for human rights and democratic freedoms.
“We stand in solidarity with the victims of this police brutality, their families, and the communities demanding accountability,” they said.

A key issue in the ASEAN protests is the Philippines’ participation in the United States’ initiative Pax Silica — a red flag for environmental groups for its components of building data centers and processing critical minerals.

The groups called on the government to “reject the Pax Silica initiative and all related projects affecting ancestral domains, respecting the right of affected indigenous peoples to free, prior, and informed consent.”
Some of the climate organizations listed as signatories in the statement have members or allies who were arrested in the protests in Manila.

The 49th ASEAN Summit, hosted by the Philippines, opened on Sunday, November 15. Hundreds who massed up for the protests in Metro Manila on Sunday were arrested. Nearly 300 people, delegates of Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan opposing the expected visit of US President Donald Trump, were arrested in Muntinlupa.
There were also arrests in Bulacan, Liwasang Bonifacio, Malate Church, and Welcome Rotonda in Quezon City, according to various local environmental and human rights groups.

“This is one of the largest mass arrests by the PNP (Philippine National Police) in recent years,” the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines noted. The network has started a donation drive for legal funds to support those arrested.
Even before the opening of the ASEAN Summit, thousands of students had already walked out and marched on the streets.
Meanwhile, Bishop Gerry Alminaza, climate champion of the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines, called on the government to “stop criminalizing the poor.”

“It is unconscionable that the poor are met with police violence when they should be met with justice, protection and action,” Alminaza, who was also in Turkey for the climate summit, said in a separate statement on Monday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
articles.summary: The Estonian government says Russia was behind the attempted sabotage, which the Kremlin denies.

blocks.text: Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".
The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.
They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.
On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.
The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.
Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.
The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.
Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.

One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.
Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."
Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.
Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.
Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

articles.title: Lawmakers, groups slam November 15 arrests: Where is maximum tolerance?
articles.summary: 'Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?' asks Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Several personalities and groups raised concerns over the massive arrests of activists and media workers during Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Pax Silica-related protests in Metro Manila on Sunday, November 15.

Progressive group Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) condemned the arrests, saying that they contradict the statement of Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Nartatez Jr.’s claim that the summit’s opening was “generally peaceful.”

“It is the police who were caught on camera kicking down arrested protesters in Manila, manhandling Lakbayan delegates in Sucat, and torturing the detainees by threatening to handcuff those who refuse to have their mugshots taken. They acted like criminal thugs who ordered the throwing of human waste at the Liwasang Bonifacio to discourage people from gathering in the park,” BAYAN said on Monday, November 16.
“The police should also explain the use of deadly weapons such as nails and ice picks in puncturing the tires of the truck to be used for the protest in Manila,” the group added.
As of Sunday, the Manila Police District said at least 11 protesters were arrested by the police in Liwasang Bonifacio.

Most of the arrests in Metro Manila happened in Muntinlupa, where PNP nabbed 276 individuals. They were from Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan, who were heading to Liwasang Bonifacio to join other groups that protested against Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s expected arrival.
Some student journalists were also among those arrested.

Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima questioned the PNP’s supposed observance of maximum tolerance and respect for freedom of expression. She called for an investigation into the reported violence and alleged denial of detainees’ access to lawyers and family members.
“Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?” said De Lima.

“We strongly condemn these arrests and the disregard for protesters’ rights. We demand a thorough investigation into the reported unlawful acts committed by the arresting officers and that those responsible be held accountable. All protesters who have been illegally detained must be released immediately!” she added.
On Sunday, several progressive groups gathered outside Camp Bagong Diwa, Taguig City, to denounce the arrests.

“Pinapakita ng pag-aresto sa humigit-kumulang tatlong daang Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan kung kaninong interes ba talaga nagsisilbi ang rehimeng US-Marcos. Sa pagbisita ni Trump, pinapakita talaga na nasa interes ng mga dayuhang bansa ang interes nila,” human rights advocate Charm Maranan said.

(The arrest of almost 300 people of Lakbayani ng Timog Katagulan shows where the interest of the US-Marcos regime truly lies. With Trump’s visit, it just shows that their interest lies in a foreign country.)
The Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan protest march kicked off in Los Baños, Laguna, on November 12, with progressive groups led by BAYAN Timog Katagalugan.

Throughout the march, activist groups and alternative media outlets reported multiple instances of harassment from the police. This included blocking the march’s path, allegedly sabotaging the protest vehicles’ tires, alleged violent manhandling of arrested protesters, and denial of the Commission on Human Rights and lawyers’ entry to police stations.

“Malinaw na ginagarantiya ng Saligang Batas ang kalayaan nating magpahayag at mapayapang magtipon. Ang kakayahan ng mamamayang pumuna at manawagan ng pagbabago ang patunay na buhay ang ating demokrasya,” said Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno.

(It’s clear that the Constitution guarantees our freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The ability of the citizens to redress their grievances and call for change is proof that our democracy is alive.)

Meanwhile, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) demanded the immediate release of individuals detained for participating in or covering the protests. The group also appealed to fellow lawyers to provide legal assistance to those arrested, calling on them to “help secure the freedom of the arrestees.”

“While we have already dispatched quick reaction teams to assist the detainees, we need more lawyers to assist them. And we are calling [on] our people’s lawyers to once again rise to the occasion. Our brave clients need brave lawyers,” said NUPL president Ephraim Cortez.
Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay also pushed for accountability from police personnel and officers involved in the reported assaults.
“Protestors must be immediately released,” Palabay asserted, urging authorities to guarantee the arrested’s access to legal counsel, relatives, and medical assistance while in custody.

On a similar note, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines also pressed authorities to stop the violence against media workers, noting the importance of peaceful assembly and press freedom.

“Journalists must be allowed to exercise their duty to cover public events, document abuses, and report the stories of those who take to the streets,” the union stated. – Ren Enano and Rhen Peñada/Rappler.com

Rena Eñano and Rhen Peñada are Rappler volunteers. Eñano is a senior literature student from Ateneo de Manila University, while Peñada is a third-year information technology student from Polytechnic University of the Philippines Sta. Rosa, Laguna Campus.

articles.title: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
articles.summary: The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

image.caption: Climate finance has been on the agenda at climate talks for several years now, and this one is no exceptionImage: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP

blocks.text: COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.
Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.
UN warns climate change could force millions to move

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."
Still a long way to go until a final draft

However, Kaiser criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was also cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft deal will be the focus of lengthy negotiations in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?

articles.title: Proposed NSW laws to allow coalmine to increase production pose ‘serious corruption risk’
articles.summary:
Bill to authorise expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, will be debated this week

  • Get our

blocks.text: A New South Wales government bill to increase coal production at a Hunter Valley coalmine creates a “serious corruption risk” for the state due to a clause that would give the resources minister “king-like” powers, the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson says.
The state parliament will this week debate legislation to allow MACH Energy to increase coal production at the Mount Pleasant mine in Muswellbrook by 32% to 16.5m tonnes per year.

The Minns government announced the bill last month after the high court ruled that an expansion of the mine was invalidly approved. The government has said the legislation is necessary to prevent 400 job losses at the site before Christmas.

Watson, the Greens and some members of the crossbench have raised concerns that a clause in the bill would give the resources minister of the day “unusually broad” powers to override other state laws.
Known as a Henry VIII clause, it would allow the minister to make regulations that could modify laws of the state as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development.
Henry VIII provisions are sometimes used by parliaments and draw their name from King Henry VIII and his style of governing by royal proclamation.
Watson is a director of the Centre for Public Integrity and Grata Fund and a former counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac).

In a legal analysis of the bill, he raised concerns that Clause 17 “explicitly places” wide powers to “make new laws (or to repeal or modify existing laws) in the hands of one person – the mining minister – and for a single coal mine owner”.
“There are real problems with this as it is known that the concentration of this kind of power in the hands of one person creates a serious corruption risk,” he wrote.

blocks.caption: Geoffrey Watson says that corruption can include ‘undue influence’ and ‘decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest’. Photograph: Dan Peled/AAP

blocks.text: He said the risk was “heightened” because the Mount Pleasant bill had been created for a single private company. He wrote that while he imputed “no bad faith at all to the current mining minister”, past experience in the state “has shown that not all ministers have acted in a manner free from improper motives”.
“Historically, we’ve seen this concentration of power into the hands of a single decision maker as posing a serious risk of corruption,” Watson told Guardian Australia.
“Now, corruption in that sense may not mean money passing hands. It also includes undue influence, decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest.”

Elaine Johnson is the director of Johnson Legal, which represented the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg) in the high court proceedings. In a separate legal opinion, she raised similar concerns there was “a very obvious corruption risk arising from Clause 17”.

She wrote that the clause gave the resources minister of the day “unfettered power to make regulations to change the application of any law of the state” to the mine, and said it could potentially affect many laws that applied to the mine, such as those that regulate noise and dust or worker safety.

The lower house is expected to debate the legislation on Tuesday, followed by the upper house later this week. The Minns government is hoping to pass the bill in what is likely to be the final sitting week before the March 2027 election.
Both Labor and Coalition lower house seats are under pressure from One Nation in the Hunter, where the mine is located.
One Nation’s NSW leader and candidate for Cessnock, Mike Newman, has described the Minns government’s bill to increase production limits at Mount Pleasant as a “Band-Aid on a bullet-wound”.

The Coalition resources spokesperson and Nationals MP for Upper Hunter, Dave Layzell, said the opposition would not oppose Labor’s legislation “in any way”. Asked about the Henry VIII clause, he said the Coalition would follow advice on the bill from the parliament’s legislation review committee which is expected on Tuesday.
after newsletter promotion
“We recognise [Labor’s] argument about the need to protect the number of jobs they are quoting.
“We agree that it is important that we fix the situation with the Mount Pleasant Mine extension.
“We cannot allow green environmental lawfare to continue to delay projects that have the support of the majority of the community, and are approved on a technical basis by the planning system.”

blocks.caption: A protest in Sydney this month opposing the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coalmine. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Greens climate spokesperson Sue Higginson said it was “the broadest” Henry VIII clause she had seen during the current parliament and the party would seek to remove it from the bill or limit its scope.
“Placing that much power in the hands of a single minister is a corruption risk the Labor government should know well,” she said.

“A tightly limited Henry VIII provision can be necessary to give effect to parliament’s decision over time, as with the recent Great Koala National Park bill, where it allowed more land to be permanently protected in the public interest as it becomes available.”

A spokesperson for the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, said the government had been clear that the purpose of its bill was to protect all permanent workers at Mount Pleasant. They said the bill had been presented transparently to parliament.
“We welcome constructive engagement on the Bill from crossbenchers and will engage with good-faith amendments as we always do,” they said.
“Any proposed regulation would be submitted to the Executive Council for approval and published transparently in the usual manner, and also subject to disallowance in the usual manner.”
They added that Henry VIII provisions had been “routinely” used in legislation for decades, including in bills the Greens had supported in this term of parliament.
The independent MP Alex Greenwich, who intends to oppose the bill as a whole, said the provision was “dangerously broad and quite unprecedented”.
“It’s especially concerning, given parliament won’t sit for six months, meaning regulations issued during that time won’t be able to be disallowed,” he said.

articles.title: Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk
articles.summary:
Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands

They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the…

blocks.text: They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the culinary-minded, but experts have now warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.

An international group of mycologists, including experts from the Royal Horticultural Society, have said many of these kits, which allow people to easily grow mushrooms at home as a delicious addition to stir-fries and other dishes, contain invasive species.

The edible golden oyster mushroom, a favourite option, has been found growing in UK forests at breakneck speed. It has now been officially classed as a high-risk invasive species because of its negative impact on woodlands.
Scientists have said the golden oyster has established itself in the wild in at least two UK forests, with the most likely pathway of introduction being escape or release from grow kits.

Native to east Asia, the mushroom species has been found to be invasive on other continents as it has wind-dispersed spores that can travel thousands of miles, making it impossible to stop its spread. It arrived in the US in 2012 and has spread across 25 states and approximately 772,200 sq miles (2m sq km). Because it establishes itself so successfully, the species has been shown to as much as halve the beneficial wood-inhabiting native fungi.

Despite its invasive nature, it is still legal to sell the golden oyster commercially, with grow kits widely available online and through large retailers. The RHS no longer exhibits the golden oyster at events, nor does it sell the mushroom in its shops, instead spotlighting native species that can be grown at home including lion’s mane.

Dr Jassy Drakulic, a senior plant pathologist at the RHS, said: “The growing public interest in fungi is something to celebrate, but as they become more widely grown and sold, we must also recognise the biosecurity risks that can accompany them. The escape of the golden oyster mushroom in the UK highlights a significant gap in how invasive fungi are managed.

“Fungi are difficult to track in the wild, living mostly unseen until they fruit, so we need stronger policies to prevent introducing species that can permanently alter native ecosystems. Developing a dedicated strategy for invasive fungi is essential if we are to safeguard biodiversity for the future.”

Invasive species are one of the world’s leading causes of biodiversity loss. A famous example in Britain is the grey squirrel. It was imported from the US in the 1800s and spread a fatal disease known as squirrelpox to the native red squirrels. As a result, red squirrels have become extinct in many parts of Britain.

Aishwarya Veerabahu, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the US, said: “Every golden oyster mushroom kit sold gives the golden oyster a chance to establish in nature and spread from there. Mushroom kits helped the golden oyster rapidly spread across the US and Canada; in less than a decade, it colonised vast areas of North America, and its full ecological impacts are still unfolding.

“Fungi are the foundation of forests and we’re beginning to understand how invasive species are impacting local biodiversity and disrupting their complex relationships. Golden oysters haven’t spread too far in the UK yet, so there’s a fighting chance of preventing it from becoming invasive. We’re asking people to hold off on buying mushroom kits to protect the UK’s fungal biodiversity and favourite native edibles.”

articles.title: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
articles.summary:
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda items, but many hope world’s three biggest nuclear powers will talk about denuclearisation

The unprecedented meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald…
articles.byline: Rebecca Bailey in Shenzhen and agencies

blocks.text: The unprecedented meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.

The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, cements Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
The topics up for discussion are far from clear but many – including the UN secretary general – are hoping that denuclearisation will be discussed between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

In a call this week, China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US state department said.
China was the last of the three powers to confirm the trilateral meeting was happening, and its statement stopped short of confirming specific agenda items.

“[The leaders] will exchange views in-depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” said the foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning. “Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along ​with managing differences and stabilising relations, serves the interests of all three countries.”
The Kremlin said “the signficance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate”.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”.

blocks.caption: People gather to watch a light show on buildings in Shenzhen, the host city for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Photograph: Wang Zhao/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: However, many analysts have warned to temper expectations of a major breakthrough.

Xi will “bask in the glow of China serving as the convener and agenda-setter”, wrote Brookings’ Ryan Hass in one such take. However, “symbolism may prove more enduring than the substance of this meeting”.
The three leaders would be approaching the talks with very different priorities, Xiaoyu Pu from the University of Nevada told the Guardian.
after newsletter promotion

China has rebuffed previous attempts to become embroiled in nuclear arms talks with ​Russia and the US, which ‌have the larger stockpiles. Trump, though, has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation, as well as the US-Israeli war in Iran. China, a top economic partner of Tehran, has sought to mediate in the conflict, and says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”.
In contrast, as feared by Kyiv, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine might not come up at all, despite Putin reportedly wanting it to.

US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, and the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.
For Xi, “much of the political benefit” will be simply in “the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table”, Peter Alexander, the Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors, told CNBC.

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the Trump administration had pushed back against Beijing’s demands that the summit be tightly scripted, with prepared statements and not much room for discussion.

Sari Arho Havrén, from the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, wrote on X: “China dislikes surprises and wants to ensure neither Trump nor Putin steals the limelight from the host. Moreover, Xi doesn’t want to be dragged into a discussion about Ukraine or anything else he is not prepared for.”

articles.title: Canada’s inflation rate flat year-over-year in October: StatsCan
articles.summary: The national inflation rate was flat on an annualized basis in October, according to data released by Statistics Canada on Monday.

image.caption: (CBC)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
The national inflation rate was flat on an annualized basis in October, according to data released by Statistics Canada on Monday.
The agency says the consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.1 per cent last month, matching the 3.1 per cent increase in September.
As of Monday morning, a Bloomberg poll of 12 economists had predicted October's CPI reading would rise an average of 3.2 per cent on an annualized basis.
More to come
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction
articles.summary: The French film star was due to start an appeal trial after being found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a Paris set.

blocks.text: French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.
On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.
"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.
It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.
"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court.
"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.
In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.
"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.

"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.

"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."
The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.

articles.title: Quebecor makes $31B offer to acquire Telus
articles.summary: Proposed deal will combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities, with Quebecor arguing the combined company would create a stronger telecom company for consumers.

image.caption: The Quebecor logo is seen at the company's head office, in Montreal in May 2024. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
Proposed deal will combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities, with Quebecor arguing the combined company would create a stronger telecom company for consumers.
Proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities
Quebecor has made a proposal worth $31 billion to take over Telus.

The telecom company said Monday in a news release it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations. Telus is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month, according to the release.
The Montreal-based company says the proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities to strengthen investment capacity and competitive positioning.
Quebecor, Canada's fourth largest telecom company, argues that acquiring Telus would create a stronger company that could better serve consumers across the country.

"This proposal will create a strong pan-Canadian competitor, able to compete on equal terms with the other national providers and to stand up to foreign companies, for the benefit of Canadians," Quebecor said in the statement.
