articles.title: Under-threat lidos get lifeline as Andy Burnham sets up fund to rebuild pools
articles.summary:
Move reflects growing demand for outdoor swimming as Britain heats up and follows campaign by MPs

Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in outdoor swimming.
Outdoor pools were built across the UK in the 1930s. The often beautiful, art deco constructions were made as a cheap way to provide access to healthy activity during the summer.

In the following decades the lidos fell into decline and by the end of the 1980s nearly two-thirds were derelict or demolished. Britain had more than 300 lidos in the 1930s but only about a third were still open in 1990. Some survivors are still at risk of closing down today and communities are fighting to keep them open.
Now, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has committed to creating a dedicated national fund to reinvigorate the UK’s lidos, after a campaign by MPs.

The move reflects the growing demand for outdoor swimming as summers in Britain heat up, and the fact that many communities do not have a place for cooling off. Better, the biggest leisure centre group in the country, which runs 10 outdoor swimming centres, said 2026 was by far its busiest year for outdoor swimming, with trips to its lidos between June and August rising by 28% to 692,471 visits.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, said the investment would be “the first dedicated fund for lidos that this country has produced” and would form part of a wider public leisure facilities programme.
MPs who have campaigned to keep lidos open in their cities welcomed news of the fund.
Andrew Pakes, the Labour MP for Peterborough, who campaigned to keep the city’s lido open after the council’s budget plans suggested it could be mothballed, said the announcement was welcome news.

This year, Peterborough’s Grade II-listed art deco lido celebrated its 90th anniversary and its best ever season, which Pakes said echoed the experience at outdoor swimming facilities in many other cities. “This makes protecting and supporting our pools even more important,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

He has been leading a group of MPs who have been calling for funding to build or reopen lidos in their local areas. “For places like Peterborough, the lido is far more than somewhere to swim. It is a much-loved part of our city’s heritage, bringing people together across generations,” he said.

The Carlisle MP, Julie Minns, who founded the campaign to save the city’s Grade II-listed Victorian and Turkish Baths, said: “These are places that bring communities together, support physical and mental wellbeing and form an important part of our shared heritage. In Carlisle, our Victorian and Turkish Baths are one of the city’s most distinctive historic buildings and have served generations of local residents.”

articles.title: USC star JuJu Watkins could change Toronto Tempo's future, providing she declares for WNBA draft
articles.summary: Most WNBA executives have long considered JuJu Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.

image.caption: USC star JuJu Watkins is the consensus No. 1 pick for next year's WNBA draft, though she has yet to declare herself eligible. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Basketball·Analysis
Most WNBA executives have long considered JuJu Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.
A generational prospect, 21-year-old wants to win NCAA title before turning pro
· for CBC Sports
· Posted: Nov 16, 2026 8:32 AM EST | Last Updated: 26 minutes ago

If you want a glimpse into the future of the WNBA, we encourage you to watch highlights from Sunday’s women’s college basketball game between the University of South Carolina and the University of Southern California. The game was marketed as “The Real SC” (both teams use “SC” as part of their athletic identity) but calling it The WNBA Draft Invitational would have been more accurate.

There were future first-round picks all across Bon Secours Wellness Arena in Greenville, S.C., including a six-pack of prospects from No. 1-ranked South Carolina (Joyce Edwards, Chloe Kitts, Tessa Johnson, Agot Makeer, Jerzy Robinson and Ashlyn Watkins). The No. 3-ranked USC star contingent included sophomore guards Jazzy Davidson, Kennedy Smith and freshman forward-guard Saniyah Hall, the top-ranked high school recruit entering the season. All of the players above are projected as first-round picks between the 2027 and 2029 WNBA drafts.

But in a game featuring future WNBA stars, there was one prospect who stood above the rest as far as name recognition and possibility — USC guard-forward JuJu Watkins, a six-foot-two senior wing with the ability to score from three levels (at the rim, mid-range and three-point distance). Most WNBA executives have long considered Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.

On Sunday, the 21-year-old Watkins showed flashes of what she can be. She has one of the most artistically pleasing pull-up jumpers in the history of women’s college basketball and unlike many prolific scorers, she attacks defences with the intensity of a starving pit bull. You win titles in the WNBA with elite front-court players and Watkins can swing seamlessly between the forward and guard spots, making her a difficult challenge for defences. Her potential is vast — she missed the entire 2025–26 season due to a torn right ACL and looks like she has not missed a beat. But the complete product is still a couple of years away. Watkins finished with 25 points on 8 of 20 shooting against South Carolina but also had five turnovers. (South Carolina’s big-game experience and deeper frontcourt talent was the difference; they held on for an 89-85 win.)

Like most WNBA executives, Toronto Tempo general manager Monica Wright Rogers watched Sunday afternoon’s game very closely. But Wright Rogers had far more stake than most. The Tempo entered Sunday night’s WNBA lottery with a 32.9 per cent chance at the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft, tied with the Houston Comets (formerly the Connecticut Sun) for the best odds .
By now you likely know what happened: Toronto landed the No. 1 pick.

items: Toronto Tempo earn No. 1 pick after winning 2027 WNBA draft lottery

blocks.text: ANEESAH CALLED IT 🇨🇦 Morrow had a feeling tonight would be special, and @TempoBasketball is walking away with the No. 1 overall pick! WNBA Draft Lottery 2027 | @StateStreetETFs SPY https://t.co/bPtvhbcgF5—WNBA

“There were no words for the emotion that filled our conference room where I was with the strategy team and our comms [communication] team,” Rogers said when asked what it was like when she saw the news on television. “Our hearts were beating out of our chest.”

One of the unique twists to the WNBA draft puzzle this year is that the top draft-eligible players in women’s college basketball can all return for another year in college because of the NCAA's new "5-in-5" eligibility rule which allows Division I and II women's basketball players up to five years of eligibility to compete in five seasons. Thus, Watkins has the option for a fifth year at USC as a medical redshirt given she missed last season with an ACL injury. Texas forward Madison Booker, Notre Dame point guard Hannah Hidalgo and LSU’s Mikaylah Williams — the consensus group right behind Watkins — can also choose to return to their American colleges.

“It makes draft planning even tougher for teams and GMs,” said Rebecca Lobo, the Naismith Basketball Hall of Famer who called South Carolina-USC for ESPN. "If JuJu Watkins enters the draft, the impact would be immense both on and off the court for Toronto. She is the type of talent you build a franchise around. Not only an incredible player but she already has a big brand that will help drive ticket sales and viewers. JuJu could be a massive cornerstone for the Tempo.”
Watkins (12) has said she wants to win a NCAA title with her hometown USC before she turns pro. (Melina Pizano/Getty Images)

Where does Watkins stand? Well, the only thing she has offered publicly is that she won’t address her draft status until after USC’s season has concluded. Watkins is L.A.-born and she has repeatedly said her dream is to win a college title in her hometown.

Wright Rogers said on Sunday night that the Tempo front office is in constant communication with college coaches and agents and that will clearly be the case here. Watkins is represented by Klutch Sports Group, which is the agency that also represents NBA star LeBron James.

“Now that we have some direction, we really can hone in on understanding the plan that these athletes have for their future,” Wright Rogers said. “It’s going to be very complicated and it may come down to the wire. Each player has about 48 hours after their last NCAA game to declare. We will stay proactively locked in.”

items: Women's pro sport drives interest for Canadian girls, not necessarily participation, report says

blocks.text: The positives for Watkins to come out in 2027 are what you’d expect. She can compete against the best players in the world, the WNBA is a better launching pad for a shot at the U.S. Olympic team, and playing in Canada will give her the opportunity to market herself not just to a city but an entire country

But here is where it gets tricky. Watkins is a high-profile U.S. college athlete and already has significant Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) deals with companies such as Nike, Gatorade, and Fanatics. Her 2026 college earnings will almost unquestionably top what she would earn in salary in the WNBA next season. (The salary for the 2027 WNBA No. 1 pick could be as high as $565,000 for next year’s top pick under the new collective bargaining agreement.) Staying in college will continue to make her wealthy.

There is also this: Watkins and her management team might want to place her in a U.S. market. They could roll the dice that her hometown L.A. Sparks (who next season have their own pick as well as the Chicago Sky’s pick) crash out and land the No. 1 pick in the 2028 draft.
Madison Booker (35) is another top prospect the Tempo will be watching. (Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

The good news is the Tempo are likely to land an all-star calibre prospect even if Watkins declines to come out. Booker is a 6-foot-1 forward who can efficiently score from both mid-range and the perimeter — the kind of player that wins you championships. She can defend power forwards given her strength in the post. So far this season she is averaging 21 points per game on 57 per cent shooting. It is very unlikely she will return to Texas.

Hidalgo is one of the best point guard prospects in years, an insanely prolific scorer and a disruptive player on defence who broke the NCAA Division I single-season steals record last season with 202. Her only flaw is size – she’s just 5-foot-7. But so far bigger guards have been unable to stop her. She is averaging an obscene 28.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 4.8 steals this season. LSU’s Williams (a 6-foot guard with a very quick release) is probably next on the list. It is still a very deep draft if everyone opts to come out outside of Watkins.
“Throughout the history of this league, getting the number one pick does alter the trajectory of your franchise,” Wright Rogers said.

There was a significant fiscal commitment from Tempo ownership to be competitive in 2026 — Toronto made Marina Mabrey and Brittany Sykes the league’s first million-dollar backcourt — but things unraveled quickly. The team was ravaged by injuries, finishing at 11-33 including losing 22 of their last 24 games. How bad did it get? The Tempo ranked first overall in games lost to in-season injuries and the quartet of Sykes, Mabrey, Nyara Sabally, and Kiki Rice — the team’s most talented players— played a total of just 78 minutes together this season.

“We are putting in the work to ensure that we don't have the situation with injuries again,” Wright Rogers said. “We're putting in a lot of time reshaping our health and performance group, putting a microscope under the group, and putting resources and the backing into that space so we won't be repeating those same injury woes that we had last season.”

items: 'Only up from here': Tempo's off-court success offers optimism after injury-ravaged inaugural campaign

blocks.text: Toronto currently has six players under contract for 2027 (Mabrey, Sykes, Kiki Rice, Julie Allemand, Aneesah Morrow and Teonni Key) and more than $4 million available in cap space. The No. 1 pick gives them roster construction options and also offers the enticement for free agents to play with a potential franchise player.

Wright Rogers did not formally say that she would pick Watkins during a post-lottery call with reporters if Watkins declares for the pros, but the Tempo boss most certainly will call her name if the star comes out. Given all of this, here is the one bit of advice we can offer as we enter the beginning of JuJu Watch:
If you are a fan of the Toronto Tempo, you should root very hard for the USC Trojans to win the NCAA women’s basketball title next spring.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Richard Deitsch is a Toronto-based writer and podcaster who previously worked for The Athletic as a media reporter as well as Sports Illustrated, where he covered seven Olympic Games among other assignments. He has also worked in radio and was an adjunct professor at Columbia University. He hosts “The Sports Media Podcast,” featuring U.S. and Canadian sports media figures.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in Poundland
articles.summary: Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’

blocks.text: David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed.
The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon.

DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York.
Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty.

Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 per bottle.
Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”.

In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades.

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland, allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties.

Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland, but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range.
after newsletter promotion

Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss.

The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham.

This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America.
The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List.
DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

articles.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
articles.summary:
• Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree

  • Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for…

blocks.text: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player it named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
articles.summary: Leaders and representatives of the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and their allies, are gathering in Manila for the bloc's biggest event of the year

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

articles.title: Ukraine launches biggest drone attack on Russia since war began: Defence ministry
articles.summary: Russian air defences intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv's biggest aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its…

image.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin listens to Russian Transport Minister Dmitry Yadrov at the Kremlin in Moscow on Monday. Ukraine has launched its biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the full-scale war began in 2022, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday. (Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/The Ass

blocks.text: World

Russian air defences intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv's biggest aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.
Russian air defences intercepted some 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine
Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some attacks in recent months.

Russia, meanwhile, has battered Ukrainian civilian areas with relentless strikes that seek to make normal daily life impossible and break public morale, especially through strikes on the power grid, as well as choking the economy.
The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of Ukrainian civilians, Western analysts and officials say.
Six people were wounded in an attack on Russia's southern Krasnodar region, according to local authorities. The town is home to the Ilsky oil refinery, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Firefighters work at the site of a cardboard factory hit by a Russian jet drone attack Monday, in Odesa, Ukraine. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)
In the Rostov region near the border with Ukraine, three people in the city of Azov, where two oil depots are located, were wounded by drones, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.
Around 600 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Most were downed far away, while 191 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital, he said.
Ukraine pushes back with long-range strikes
The strikes on Russia serve multiple purposes for Ukraine.

They have repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, which are an economic mainstay for Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed late Sunday that Ukrainian attacks have disabled more than 55 per cent of Russia's oil refining capacity.

Russian officials didn't comment on that claim, and independent verification wasn't possible. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes' economic impact, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly one per cent of its gross domestic product.

Ukrainian officials are keen, too, to make Russians feel the war at home, while mid-range strikes are disrupting Russia's front-line supply routes and hampering Moscow's efforts to get momentum on the battlefield, analysts say.

items: U.S. envoys talk to Zelenskyy in Dublin, after prior sitdown with Putin in Moscow
Russia-Ukraine talks mediated by U.S. end with news of 'good momentum,' large-scale prisoner swap

blocks.text: Kyiv says newly imposed speed limits on the U.S.-made Starshield system, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, have weakened Ukraine's air defenses. Ukrainian forces say they are adapting to that by launching pre-emptive attacks that hit Russian weapons production plants and sites that Russia uses to launch drone and missile attacks.
Kyiv also wants to show its supporters that it is still in the fight, as Moscow tries to depict its victory in Ukraine as inevitable and U.S.-mediated talks make no impact on the war.
There was no clear picture of the extent of damage caused by Ukrainian strikes in Russia. Moscow-based and local officials rarely provide details.
Zelenskyy calls Russian strikes 'brutal'
Ukrainians are bracing for what could be the hardest winter since the war began, as Russia repeatedly batters the power grid and denies civilians heat, light and running water.

Russian strikes on power lines and substations in the southern Zaporizhzhia and central Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Monday.
Zelenskyy says the Russian strategy is to bombard specific areas for days, flattening energy infrastructure.
Since the start of September, for example, the central Dnipro region has endured 131 strikes, while the Kyiv region around the capital has witnessed 125, he said.
Russian attacks violate Trump's 'energy ceasefire', says Zelenskyy
One person was killed and three were injured in a Monday morning strike on Dnipro, local officials said.
Just over the past week, Russia has launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine, according to Zelenskyy.
They are "brutal strikes that are difficult to counter," he said on social media.

Four people were killed and three more injured in Russian shelling of towns and villages in the Donetsk region over the past day, said Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration.

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Monday said relations among members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are sustained through cooperation to strengthen peace and opportunities, highlighting the Filipino term "kapwa."

"There is something of kapwa in the ASEAN story. We remain different nations with our own histories, interests, and aspirations. "There will be a group of people, excellent [and] creative people who will definitely be showcasing the Philippines of its best," she added.

articles.title: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'
articles.summary: China says presidents Xi, Trump and Putin are going to have "in-depth discussions on global peace." Ukraine, Iran and denuclearization could also feature in the talks.

image.caption: Trump, Xi and Putin are set to hold their first-ever trilateral meetingImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Beijing said on Monday the leaders of the US, Russia and China will discuss "world peace" in their first trilateral summit in China this week.
Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are due to meet in the southern Chinese city Shenzhen on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
China provided few details about the talks, but said they would involve "in-depth discussions on preserving global peace and promoting stability in relations."
"It will be of ground-breaking significance," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news briefing on Monday, hours after Beijing confirmed the meeting.
Ukraine unlikely to be discussed
US President Donald Trump has previously said the meeting will be "interesting."
"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," he told reporters at a Florida airport on November 8.
Trump, Xi, Putin to hold first-ever trilateral meeting
In his brief remarks Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine.
According to a report published by the Wall Street Journal last month, Putin wanted the talks to broker a Ukraine peace agreement that would serve Moscow's interests.
US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, AFP news agency reported.
Following his visit to China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi appeared irritated when asked whether the trilateral talks would cover Ukraine.
"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told ARD earlier this month.

blocks.caption: The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saidImage: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with Putin during the talks.
"Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," he said.
Is an agreement on denuclearization possible?
Washington wants China included in future nuclear arms control deals, but Beijing insists the US and Russia must first reduce their arsenals.
China previously rejected Trump's proposal for broader disarmament talks following the expiration of a US-Russia nuclear treaty in February.

But according to the US State Department, in a call this week, top diplomats Wang Yi and Marco Rubio "agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization."
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that if the three leaders "commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearization, it will be a great achievement for the world."
Where does the Iran war stand?
The Iran war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing some de-escalation although major issues remain unresolved.
Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.
Iran's regime: Inside the system protecting its rulers
Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to produce a durable settlement to the conflict.
As one of Iran's key economic partners, China has repeatedly sought to mediate in the conflict.
Beijing, says avoiding escalation is a "top priority."
It hosted leaders and diplomats from various Middle Eastern countries in recent weeks in an effort to persuade the parties to return to the negotiating table.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.summary:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine

Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a…

blocks.text: Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion

Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.

Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
articles.summary: The poet, writer and diplomat died in Europe in 1974 having been forced to leave his native country.

blocks.text: The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.
His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.
Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.
The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.
His son, whose name is also Miguel Ángel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."
Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.
Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.

Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.
Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.
Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.

But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.
At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".
The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from Père Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo Arévalo, was elected in 2023.
Arévalo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".

"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said Arévalo, whose father Juan José appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older Arévalo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

articles.title: CICC warns vs. posts 'seemingly' promoting violence amid ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: The CICC on Monday said it is monitoring online content that "seemingly" encourages violence amid ongoing protests as the country hosts the 2026 ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 8:34pm

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Monday said it is monitoring online content that "seemingly" encourages violence amid ongoing protests as the country hosts the 2026 ASEAN Summit.

“We respect the public’s right to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, and to seek redress from the government. But these freedoms should never be used as justification to incite violence or threaten public safety,” said CICC executive director Renato Paraiso in a statement.
The agency said it identified individuals whose online posts "seemingly promote or incite violence" in connection to the protests.
The CICC added that it is still assessing the credibility of the said posts.

"While the government recognizes the public’s right to air grievances and participate in peaceful protests, it will not tolerate attempts to incite violence or provoke unrest through online platforms," the agency added.
Over 200 protesters from Southern Tagalog were arrested in Sucat, Parañaque, during a protest caravan and were brought to Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City as ASEAN Summit 2026 opened on Sunday.
Among the apprehended individuals, 19 are reportedly minors. The Southern Police District, however, said the minors were rescued rather than arrested.
Various organization have condemned the arrests and the alleged violent dispersal of protesters in Metro Manila on Sunday. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Man sentenced over 'horrific' attempted murder of three children
articles.summary: Riad Bouchaker was sentenced after the attempted murder of three children in November 2023.

blocks.text: The attack took place outside Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire in Parnell Square, shortly after 13:40 local time on 23 November.

A group of 13 children, aged five and six, were lined up on Parnell Square waiting to go to their afterschool provision. Childcare worker Leanne Flynn was helping a little boy zip up his jacket when Bouchaker pulled his knife on the children.
A five-year-old girl was left with a lifelong brain injury after being stabbed in the heart.
Now eight, she is non-verbal and can only communicate by blinking, uses a wheelchair and has to be fed through a tube in her stomach as she cannot swallow safely by herself.
The judge said the child will never live independently and that her life, and the lives of her family, had been permanently altered.

He also noted that Flynn suffered life-threatening injuries, including a collapsed lung and the loss of a spleen, as well as profound psychological consequences and her services not being available to children.
The judge said she had acted fearlessly to protect the children and hoped she could return to work in the future, but said the possibility of such remains an unanswered question.
Judge Hunt said this was an unprecedented, highly unusual case involving a sudden, ferocious, sustained attack on young children and their childcare worker.
He said he had to mark the exceptional gravity of the offending against very young children and their carer, with a lethal weapon leading to consequences of the utmost gravity.
He said the circumstances were uniquely horrific and marked a profound assault on the most fundamental values protected by the criminal law.
The judge said the children happened to be selected because they were there and he was not yet sure what inference could be drawn from how Bouchaker found himself at their collection point.
At an earlier hearing, the court heard he received brain surgery in 2021 and a portion of his skull was removed, leaving a part of his brain vulnerable.
He suffered a head injury when members of the public intervened during the Parnell Square attack, after which he received hospital treatment for a month.

His defence team, which the judge ordered cannot be named due to safety concerns, said Bouchaker's cognitive function, memory, concentration, communication and decision-making were affected as a result of the impairment.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction
articles.summary:
French actor apologises to two women he was convicted of assaulting on a film set in 2021

The French actor Gérard Depardieu…

blocks.text: The French actor Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set, and has for the first time apologised to the victims.
“I was found guilty. I hear it and I accept this conviction,” Depardieu, 77, said in a written statement. “I address my deep and sincere apologies to those who suffered.”
The actor, who has made more than 200 films and TV series, wrote: “For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour.”
He said he accepted that remarks and “some of my gestures” were not “without consequences”, particularly because he held a powerful position in the entertainment industry.
Depardieu said he had never intended to hurt the women he encountered but had “come to understand that intention changes nothing about the harm caused”.
He said times had changed and that he belonged “to a world that no longer exists”.

At a trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021.
His suspended sentence will now stand and his name must be added to France’s sex offender register.

The set dresser, named in the media as Amélie, said outside the Paris appeal court on Monday: “I waited for years for this apology.” She said she would have preferred if Depardieu had attended court to deliver it in person.
The assistant director, named in the media as Sarah, said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”

Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.
Depardieu had previously denied all allegations of sexual assault. He told last year’s trial that the media had used allegations against him to damage his reputation.
He attacked the #MeToo movement as well as women who had staged protests outside venues during his concert tour at the time of the allegations. “This movement is going to become a terror,” he said.

The trial also set an important legal precedent when the judge ruled that Depardieu’s defence lawyer, Jérémie Assous, had been “excessively harsh” to the two women in court, saying they were not real victims and were liars.
Assous had said the women were working for the cause of “rabid feminism” and called their lawyers hysterical, “abject and stupid” and described them as having an “unbearable voice”.
The judge awarded the complainants compensation for being further victimised by Depardieu’s defence during the trial, ordering Depardieu to pay each woman €1,000 (£835).
The court had heard there was a “system of impunity” around Depardieu, with film industry insiders staying silent to keep cashing in on his name.

Depardieu has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.
In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

In December 2023, when Depardieu was under formal investigation for rape and sexual assault in the Arnould case and also facing scrutiny over sexist comments revealed in a TV documentary, the French president defended him, saying “he makes France proud”.
Asked at the time about stripping Depardieu of a state award, Emmanuel Macron said: “You will never see me participate in a manhunt … I hate that type of thing.”

articles.title: Germany, EU states open talks on Rwanda deportation scheme
articles.summary: The move follows approval of EU regulations that ease deportations and allow hubs to be set up outside the bloc. A similar scheme by the UK government fell apart over legal issues.

image.caption: The European Union has struggled to find a migration policy that satisfies all member statesImage: Daniel Kubirski/IMAGO

blocks.text: A group of five EU member states, including Germany, will begin talks on a new scheme to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, the Austrian government said on Monday.
A plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — back in September.
Monday's announcement comes after the EU introduced new regulations to speed up deportations and allow the establishment of hubs outside of the bloc.
What do we know about the EU deportation hub scheme?
Rwanda was had not been officially named as the chosen country, but people who had been briefed on the ongoing negotiations spoke to Reuters and AFP news agencies.
The central African country had also acknowledged being in "preliminary discussions" with the group of states.
Rwanda had also been the intended destination for a similar plan set up under the UK's former Conservative government that subsequently collapsed in UK courts.
'Migration paradox': How borders, aid drive human movement
However, the new EU scheme differs from the British one in that it is only intended for migrants who have exhausted all other legal avenues within the European Union.
Migration hubs have been seen by governments as a means to visibly show that they are taking action on migration amid surging anti-migrant sentiment and rising support for the far right.
What are the criticisms of the deportation hub plans?

While the leaders of the five countries said the scheme would comply with EU law, that has not protected them from criticism, especially over the plan to send migrants to a country with which they have no connection.
The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks."
Claims that the scheme is meant as a deterrence have been rejected by researchers who say there is no evidence that deterrence works.

"Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or ⁠change ​route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices," said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a ​research institute that collects data along migration routes.

The choice to pick Rwanda has also been controversial, with the government President Paul Kagame in particular being accused of suppressing dissent and supporting the M23 rebel group in the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad," said Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye.
Rwanda unscathed in failed UK migration deal

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Clark’s billions demand public accounting
articles.summary: Joshua Bingcang’s transfer from the BCDA to PEZA leaves a massive public accounting unfinished

blocks.text: Joshua Bingcang’s move from BCDA to PEZA leaves unanswered questions over Clark International Airport’s concession returns and asset valuations, alongside procurement, financing, and tax issues surrounding the New Clark City sports complex. While leadership changes neither prove wrongdoing nor absolve officials, true accountability demands opening the books to show whether taxpayers secured a fair bargain.
Joshua Bingcang’s transfer from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) to the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) leaves a massive public accounting unfinished.

blocks.caption: BCDA. Former Bases Conversion and Development Authority president and CEO Engineer Joshua Bingcang, in Makati City on March 9, 2026. Rappler

blocks.text: While his successor Ariel Nepomuceno now inherits the institutional duty to explain BCDA’s transactions, a simple changing of the guard does not settle the questions raised by state auditors and government agencies on how government funds were handled.

Establishing public accountability begins with examining the roles officials actually held. BCDA’s 2023 annual report identifies Bingcang as New Clark City’s overall project manager during his tenure as senior vice president, placing him in charge of business strategies and construction oversight.

He also chaired the special bids and awards committee for Clark airport operations and maintenance. While holding these positions does not prove personal wrongdoing or confirm his sign-off on every specific transfer or payment, it squarely justifies scrutinizing the recommendations he made while steering these multi-billion-peso ventures.

An airport concession is worth far more than the terminal it operates, just as a sports complex costs more than its concrete and steel. At Clark, a true public accounting must capture the land, commercial contracts, financing obligations, and tax responsibilities underpinning the infrastructure. Official records raise pointed questions about these contributions, making documentary transparency all the more essential.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] Clark’s billions demand public accounting

blocks.text: Consider the 25-year concession for Clark International Airport, operated by the Luzon International Premiere Airport Development Corp. (LIPAD). Bringing together Philippine corporate and aviation players—Filinvest Development Corp., JG Summit Holdings Inc., and Philippine Airport Ground Support Solutions Inc.—alongside Singaporean expertise via Changi Airports Philippines, LIPAD manages a vast commercial footprint.

According to the Clark International Airport Corp. (CIAC), the concession covers 759 hectares and includes 110 transferred lease agreements. Although these figures describe operating coverage and transferred contracts rather than an outright sale of state land, existing tenants and leases carry substantial economic value that the government’s returns must accurately reflect.

BCDA maintains that the government receives an 18.25% revenue share plus P500 million annually for 20 years—a P10-billion stream before discounting or examining contractual qualifications. Yet numbers in isolation tell an incomplete story. Without weighing those receipts against the commercial rights transferred, investment obligations, and retained public risks, it is impossible to establish whether taxpayers secured a favorable bargain or an undervalued concession.

Underlying asset valuations complicate the picture further. A CIAC audit-action report describes separate negotiations over assigning assets to BCDA for the LIPAD concession. In June 2025, BCDA reported that 40 buildings valued at P934 million were already recorded in its books—a move CIAC said occurred without its knowledge, prompting it to contest BCDA’s recording of the passenger terminal and crash-fire-and-rescue buildings that CIAC itself financed.

Meanwhile, seven other buildings worth approximately P478 million were excluded from the proposed assignment after CIAC clarified it did not own them under existing leases. By September 2025, BCDA’s recommended P263.73-million assignment figure stood sharply against the P777.12-million net book value under CIAC review.

Different asset coverage and accounting treatments might explain those figures without establishing a financial loss, and asset assignment to BCDA must be distinguished from LIPAD’s operational use, but the public deserves a reconciled ledger.

blocks.caption: SEA GAMES. New Clark City’s athletic stadium built for the 30th Southeast Asian Games in 2019. Rappler file

blocks.text: The Southeast Asian Games sports facilities at New Clark City present a distinct set of questions involving a different partner and agreement. While the Philippine Competition Commission confirmed that Malaysian firm MTD Capital Berhad’s unsolicited proposal went through a competitive challenge, and BCDA’s financial statements show that government acquisition of the facilities—with an option to shorten repayment—was contemplated by the agreement, acquisition alone establishes no improper buyback. (Read Rappler’s special report on this controversy by clicking these links below:

items: BCDA, Malaysian firm ink questionable P11-billion SEA Games deal
OGCC flagged non-bidding of BCDA’s New Clark sports facilities
How BCDA’s multi-billion New Clark deal slipped through

blocks.text: However, the Commission on Audit (COA) questioned the procurement route itself, finding that sports facilities originally conceptualized by BCDA were negotiated into an unsolicited proposal, granting MTD an “undue advantage.”

BCDA disputed this finding, defending the integrity of its Swiss challenge. Resolving these competing positions requires opening up to public view the original proposal, negotiated changes, and challenge documents. (Read more stories on the SEA Games controversy by clicking these links below:

items: Bloated SEA Games budget and other exposés
P1.5 billion worth of SEA Games funds will not undergo public bidding
Drilon questions P50-million ‘kaldero’ for 2019 SEA Games

blocks.text: The financial breakdown also warrants closer inspection. BCDA’s published figures put total payment at P9.539 billion: P8.510 billion for the sports facilities, P579 million in financing costs, and P450 million in ICT (Information and Communications Technology) variations.

These additions are not all interest or automatic evidence of overpricing. BCDA defended a 7.5% financing rate under an arrangement where savings below that benchmark would be shared 90:10 between the government and MTD. Settlement records should verify actual borrowing costs and confirm whether any credited savings materialized.

Tax compliance adds another unresolved thread. An audit done in 2020 recorded payments of P5.145 billion in December 2019 and P4.394 billion in April 2020, flagging P343 million in taxes withheld but not remitted to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), alongside P274.613 million in required withholding taxes never deducted from the later payment. Management explained that the venture was not yet fully incorporated or BIR-registered while anticipating PEZA tax incentives, citing missing incorporation approvals and promising a resolution in 2021.

Auditors maintained that the withholding obligation still applied. Instead of relying on unsupported assertions of continuing nonpayment, the relevant focus today should be what registrations, remittances, and corrective actions actually took place afterward.

Legal developments offer no shortcuts to accountability. An earlier complaint involving then-BCDA chief Vince Dizon and others was dismissed for insufficient evidence in December 2021, a ruling the Ombudsman announced it would review in July 2026. (READ: NBI probes 2019 SEA Games: What we know so far)

blocks.caption: How Cayetano, Dizon got ‘cleared’ in 2019 SEA Games controversy

blocks.text: Neither development establishes liability for Bingcang, who became BCDA president in 2023—well after the original award and payments. Individual responsibility cannot be inferred from a job title alone. It requires tracing the documentary record to identify who proposed each arrangement, evaluated its financial terms, and authorized its implementation.

Ultimately, an institution’s account of benefits must be tested against its contractual commitments and actual receipts, payments, and recoveries. Both the airport and the sports facilities must be assessed through their separate contracts and documented obligations. (READ: Auditors flag P290-M Clark air traffic control tower project delays, cost overruns)
Publishing reconciled asset schedules, procurement justifications, financing calculations, and tax resolutions would allow the public to evaluate these bargains for themselves.
The real test is whether the government can demonstrate that it properly valued its contribution, obtained adequate returns, and enforced the protections written into its agreements. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘When the sun came out it felt like it opened a scar’ – This is climate breakdown
articles.summary:
When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story

Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan

Disaster: Pakistan…
articles.byline: Imran Lodhi, as told to Morgan Krakow

items: Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan
Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall

blocks.text: Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.

blocks.caption: Imran Lodhi immediately rallied friends to help victims of the devastating flooding across Pakistan in 2022. Photograph: Zoral Naik

blocks.text: I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.

We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.

When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.

Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.

The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.

blocks.caption: Families displaced by flooding in Balochistan province were forced to live in tents on causeways and other higher ground. Photograph: Fida Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.

One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”

It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.

blocks.caption: Flooding in the historic city of Sehwan in September 2022. The climate crisis made monsoon rainfall more intense. Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

blocks.text: We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.

The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.

A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.

blocks.caption: People use a raft to navigate a flooded district of Hyderabad, Pakistan, in August 2022.  Photograph: Akram Shahid/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.

So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.

blocks.caption: Children take refuge in the grounds of a school after flooding in Jacobabad. Exceptional monsoon rainfall from June to October 2022 killed more than 1,700 people in Pakistan. Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

blocks.text: Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.
When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.
The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.

The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers use a boat to transport children after flooding in Dera Ghazi Khan, Punjab province, in August 2022.  Photograph: Shahid Saeed Mirza/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.

I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.

There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?
I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.

articles.title: Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms
articles.summary: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp has expressed his discontent with Gianni InfantinoImage: Martin Agüera/kolbert-press/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job."

On Sunday, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp became the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA. But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.
"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."
Why Germans don't flaunt their flag

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.
Asia backtracks despite Infantino scandals

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.
Tashima and Vega the early candidates

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

blocks.caption: Kozo Tashima is one of only two confirmed candidates to run against InfantinoImage: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (AFC) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.
UEFA still searching for unity candidate

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

articles.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, seen here with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in January, is expected to meet with Xi again this week in Shenzhen. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
PM to meet this week in China with President Xi Jinping

Carney's comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

"We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market," Carney told reporters in Cambodia. "That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions."

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

items: Canada reaches tariff-quota deal with China on EVs, canola
Chinese-made electric vehicles start arriving in Canada

blocks.text: Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: "It's not leverage. But action, reaction."

"If they're not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities," Carney said of Canada's auto workers and manufacturing assets. "Canada is going to move forward either way."

Canada and China reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. Above, a BYD Seagull electric vehicle is shown at a Beijing auto show in April. (Xiaoyu Yin/Reuters)

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.
'Not just kit cars'

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labour standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
"It's not just about kit cars," he said. "There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved."

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada's auto industry and create jobs.

items: Carney says Canada will only sign a U.S. trade deal that includes viable auto sector
Canada not in a 'position right now' to agree to U.S. trade deal, Carney says

blocks.text: The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the centre of Canada's auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump's tariffs have disrupted Canada's auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ont., to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

articles.title: Jensen Huang allies campaign to reinstate the former Nvidia boss
articles.summary: Tech leaders, including Elon Musk, are among those backing a campaign to "Bring Jensen Back".

blocks.text: Allies of Jensen Huang are trying to rally support for the former Nvidia boss to get his job back after resigning last week over a scandal involving extramarital affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, are among those backing a campaign to get the AI chip giant's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after the emergence of two affairs, one of whom was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.

An open letter calling for Nvidia's board to give Huang his job back while an internal probe is conducted has received more than 175,000 signatures, including Musk and Sweeney, according a website named "Stand with Jensen".
The campaign group said it is made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.

"We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," the letter said.
Allies of the ex-Nvidia boss wrote they were "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, this time allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to Financial Times., external
The newspaper quoted one ally saying that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being convened to lobby for the former Nvidia boss's reinstatement.
A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

While President Donald Trump recently spoke in glowing terms about Huang, the scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while the Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost," he posted on X., external
He later added: "If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through."
If Huang was reinstated, it would face scrutiny from Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at Nvidia's helm.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.
