articles.title: Five EU countries expected to announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.

blocks.text: Five EU countries are expected to announce the creation of a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, according to diplomatic sources, part of a broader push to boost deportations and curb irregular migration.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a "return hub" located in the landlocked east-central African country's capital Kigali.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of such hubs outside of the bloc.

It is understood the scheme would only apply to asylum seekers who had exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the EU, unlike a scrapped 2022 British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed.
Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually scrapped by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
In August, Rwanda confirmed it had begun "preliminary discussions" with several European states.
The Rwanda hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency.
The EU countries reportedly expressed hope that a centre would be running in 2027. The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

articles.title: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest
articles.summary:
Broadcaster TV3 appears to cut footage of Thai drag performers and gay Philippine jury spokesperson

Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first…

blocks.text: Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.

Footage circulating online of the contest, which was won by the Philippines’ Carmelle, showed the first of two cuts during the voting in Saturday’s final in Bangkok, when the Philippines’ spokesperson, Vice Ganda, awarded the Philippine jury’s points.

Vice Ganda is gay and identifies as non-binary. The comedian is among the biggest stars on Philippine television, has fronted the country’s most watched daytime show, and has campaigned for LGBTQ+ acceptance at home.
Announcing a national jury’s points is one of the most visible roles in a Eurovision final. Each country’s spokesperson appears in turn to reveal how their jury has ranked the other entries.
While the international feed showed Vice Ganda announcing that the Philippine jury had given its 12 points, the maximum, to the Malaysian entrant, Aina Abdul, TV3 viewers saw only the scoreboard.
Separate footage shows part of the show’s opening number showcasing Thai culture, in which drag performers appeared on street food carts, replaced with a wide shot taken from rehearsals.
Eurovision fans accused the channel of “censorship”. The Guardian has not been able to review TV3’s broadcast independently as its livestream is no longer available online.
Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision song contest, said: “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation, the producers of the show, to seek clarification and ask them to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why this happened.
“This appears to be isolated to the Malaysian broadcast of the show, and all other transmissions were not altered.”

Voxovation said in a statement that it was aware of the concerns raised and was “looking into the matter with the broadcaster to establish the circumstances … We are working with the Malaysian broadcaster to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Neither the EBU nor Voxovation said whether the contest’s participation agreement required broadcasters to carry the show unedited or what the consequences would be if one did not.
The Guardian has asked Media Prima, Malaysia’s largest media group and TV3’s owner, for comment.

This is not the first time the wider Eurovision song contest has faced allegations of censorship. In May 2018 the EBU terminated its partnership with the Chinese streaming service Mango TV after it dropped the Irish and Albanian entries and blurred a rainbow flag in the audience, saying such censorship was not in line with its “values of universality and inclusivity”.

Asked before Saturday’s final how the EBU’s commitment to its values squared with the laws in Malaysia and Bangladesh, the other competing country where same-sex relations are criminalised, the EBU’s head of communications, Dave Goodman, said the contest’s values were “non-negotiable”.
Malaysia has some of the harshest anti-LGBTQ+ laws in Asia, with oral and anal sex being punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

Rights groups have warned of a hardening climate. In November last year, authorities raided a men-only spa in Kuala Lumpur and detained more than 200 men, though no charges followed. And in 2022, police raided an LGBTQ+ Halloween party in the capital and arrested 20 people.

In 2023, a festival appearance by the British band the 1975, whose singer criticised the country’s homophobic laws and kissed a male bandmate on stage, led to the event being cancelled and prompted tighter entry rules for foreign performers.
TV3 has faced pressure over LGBTQ+ visibility before. In February 2025, it apologised after male guests arrived at a red carpet event in clothing resembling women’s dress.

articles.title: DOJ warns Elizabeth Warren over Trump investigations – US politics live

Letter to likely chair of Senate Banking Committee is latest warning to Democrats about their potential plans following midterms success

Hello and welcome to the US politics live…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 19m agoDOJ warns senator Warren about potential Trump-related probes

blocks.text: DOJ warns senator Warren about potential Trump-related probes
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, was warned by he US Department of ⁠Justice of potential “significant legal consequences” if she fails ⁠to preserve records related to ⁠investigations into ​president Donald Trump.
It is the latest warning sent by the justice department to congressional Democrats about their potential plans to investigate the ⁠administration or Trump associates, Reuters reported.

Trump last week ordered the department to look into Democratic lawmakers for “threatening” people, and US attorney-general Todd Blanche subsequently indicated that ⁠his agency was prepared to battle congressional Democrats.

In a letter to Warren, US attorney Aaron ​Reitz in Houston told the Massachusetts Democrat ‌she appeared “eager to wield your ‌future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of president Trump’s private associates”.
Reitz told ‌her to preserve materials “relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights”.

Notices to preserve records can presage investigations. Warren’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reitz shared the letter on social media and Trump reposted it to his Truth Social account several hours later.

Warren and other Democrats have signaled ‌that when their party takes control of Congress in January, they plan to investigate large corporations, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Elon ​Musk, the world’s richest person, among others.
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days.

Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances. Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.

US air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but transportation secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normal by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024. Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.

articles.title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
articles.summary:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican…

blocks.text: Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.
Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

blocks.caption: A sign in Shenzen’s business district promoting the Apec summit. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA

blocks.text: Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine, which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China, which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.
after newsletter promotion

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.
Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum. “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

articles.title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
articles.summary:
Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza

The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m…

blocks.text: The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.
The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians wait to cross a checkpoint in Mughraqa in central Gaza in January 2025. Photograph: Eyad Baba/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.
It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.
However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

blocks.caption: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos speaks at the America Business Forum in Miami last year. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP

blocks.text: They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”
An embrace of big tech
In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.
The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

blocks.caption: A surveillance camera is pictured at a checkpoint in the Palestinian city of Hebron in 2021. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.
‘The plan was to migrate everything’

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.
The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”
A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.
The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

items: Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

articles.title: SC declares parts of Magna Carta of Seafarers unconstitutional. So what?
articles.summary: The SC voids the rule that requires seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before a court

items: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional a provision in the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers that required seafarers to post a bond while their shipowners appealed labor dispute victories, citing violations of due process and equal protection.

The Court also voided other provisions related to the regulation of lawyer-seafarer contracts and the use of public funds for bond premiums, emphasizing that the regulation of legal practice is under the Supreme Court's exclusive authority.
While some provisions regarding maritime education were upheld, the Court affirmed the need for reasonable regulations to ensure quality training and compliance with international standards.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional a provision in the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. Groups had previously criticized the provision as discriminatory because it requires seafarers who initially win in cases to post a bond while their shipowner or manpower agency is appealing the decision.
The High Court likewise voided other provisions in the law and other issuances related to it.

In a decision penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh, the High Court en banc partially granted the five consolidated petitions challenging the legality of Republic Act (RA) No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. The petitions likewise questioned certain provisions of the law’s Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR), as well as related government issuances.
Petitioners include labor lawyer Sonny Matula, several seafarers, labor organizations, and maritime educational institutions.

“The Court emphasized that although the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers was enacted to advance the welfare of Filipino seafarers, all legislative measures must conform to the Constitution. The law therefore remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void,” said the ruling penned by Singh.

blocks.caption: What is the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers?

blocks.text: Signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in 2024, the Magna Carta clarifies the rights of Filipino seafarers — just working conditions, right to organize, and freedom from discrimination.

The ruling voided the law’s Section 59 or the requirement for Filipino seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before courts. The bond requirement was supposedly meant to ensure restitution or monetary reward, should the case be subsequently reversed or modified.
Groups challenged this because the only chance for seafarers to be reimbursed for the bond they post is if they win their case.
The High Court sided with the petitioners and ruled that this bond requirement violates due process and equal protection clauses under the 1987 Constitution.
The SC said this rule imposes a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments, and subjects them to a disadvantage “not similarly imposed on other workers.”

“While recognizing the State’s interest in preventing ambulance chasing and protecting the maritime industry against unrestituted awards, the Court found that these objectives did not justify the challenged restriction on the execution of monetary awards,” said the SC.

The SC also declared unconstitutional the authorization to use the Department of Migrant Workers’ (DMW) Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund to pay for the bond premiums. The High Court said this mechanism failed the constitutional requirement that public funds should be used for a public purpose, as found under Section 29(1), Article VI of the 1987 Constitution.

“Sections 4 and 5, Rule III of Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Order No. 247, Series of 2025, were likewise declared unconstitutional and void insofar as they implemented the bond requirement,” the High Court added.

blocks.caption: SC declares parts of Magna Carta of Seafarers unconstitutional.  So what?

blocks.text: “Great, at last, our petition was resolved by the SC. This a good news. This is victory for workers especially the seafarers,” Matula told Rappler.

“We argued [that Section 59] is discriminatory. It violates the equal protection clause of the 1987 Constitution because land-based workers do not face this requirement. We also contend that it creates an unfair financial burden on sick, injured, or unemployed seafarers,” he added.

The SC also struck down Section 60 of RA No. 12021, as well as Section 4 of RA No. 10706, or the Seafarers Protection Act. The High Court said these provisions regulated the practice of law, which is a violation of Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
Petitioners challenged these sections because they regulate lawyer-seafarer contracts and cap contingent legal fees at 10%.

“Petitioners argue that this rule (Section 60) usurps the exclusive constitutional power of the Supreme Court to regulate the practice of law and may restrict seafarers’ access to competent legal counsel,” said Matula.

The SC explained that while the legislative department may create laws to protect seafarers from lawyers’ alleged abusive practices like ambulance chasing, among others, the regulation of lawyers’ professional conduct and the practice of the law remains under the High Court’s exclusive authority.
Ambulance chasing refers to the practice of lawyers of soliciting professional employment.

Apart from the said provisions, the SC also declared unconstitutional Section 1, Rule XXII, of the law’s IRR. This is because it applies Section 59 to monetary rewards from complaints filed on or after the magna carta’s effectivity.

“The Court found that the implementing provision contravened Section 94 of the law, which expressly preserves the rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers before its effectivity. It reiterated that administrative regulations must conform to the statute they implement and cannot diminish rights expressly preserved by law,” said the SC.
Meanwhile, the Court denied the challenge to the law’s Sections 75, 76, and 78, because it said they do not violate constitutional guarantee of academic freedom.

items: Section 75 – States that the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) has jurisdiction over maritime education in the country.
Section 76 – Requires shipboard training for international maritime degree programs. MARINA determines the applicability of the training, including the duration.

Section 78 – Requires maritime higher educational institutions offering international maritime degree programs to have their own training ships, simulators, or related technologies. This also requires them to enter into agreements with local or international shipping companies, shipowners, or agencies for the shipboard training program of students or cadets.

blocks.text: The Philippine Association of Maritime Institutions, Inc. and other maritime educational institutions questioned these provisions before the SC.
In its ruling, the SC said academic freedom ensures the autonomy of higher educational institutions, but this freedom does not exempt them from reasonable regulations.

“[The Court] found that the challenged provisions established minimum regulatory standards intended to ensure the quality of maritime education, the competency of Filipino seafarers, and compliance with applicable international maritime standards. Particularly, the requirements relating to enrollment and available shipboard training opportunities were considered reasonable measures to address the availability of practical training for maritime students,” said the SC.
“The prohibition against charging tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third party providers was likewise sustained as a measure against unjustified charges,” it added.

blocks.caption: More Filipino seafarers are being abandoned at sea

blocks.text: The petitioners also questioned the legislative process leading to the magna carta’s passage. But the SC denied this specific challenge and upheld the procedural validity of the law.
It found that Congress complied with the constitutional requirements in passing a law, such as the three-reading rule under Article VI of the Constitution.

“The Court likewise upheld the President’s Certification of Urgency and recognized the authority of the Bicameral Conference Committee to reconcile differences between the House and Senate versions of the proposed legislation,” the SC added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 17 dead
articles.summary: The shootings in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng highlight South Africa's struggle to curb violent crime.

blocks.text: South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.

Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.
Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.
South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.
Police say they responded to reports of a shooting ⁠outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.
Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.

"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.
The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.

They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.
Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.

"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.
Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.
In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.
In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.
Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.

According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.
Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

articles.title: South Africa: 17 killed in separate mass shooting incidents
articles.summary: Police are investigating two mass shooting incidents in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal provinces. There has been a growing trend of mass shooting incidents making headlines in recent years.

image.caption: Around 60 people are killed in the country on average a day, according to police statisticsImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: At least 17 people have been killed in two separate shooting incidents in South Africa, police said on Monday.
South Africa is battling extremely high levels of violent crime with around 60 people killed every day.

blocks.caption: In one of the incidents, 9 people were found with gunshot wounds in an informal settlement near PretoriaImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: What we know about the latest incidents
The South African Police Service (SAPS) said in a statement that nine bodies were found early on Monday in an informal settlement outside of the capital Pretoria in Gauteng province.
A police spokeswoman said that officers were alerted to the scene at 07:30 a.m. (0530 UTC/GMT) and on arrival found six dead males and three dead females inside a shack, all with gunshot wounds.
Police said a motive for the shooting had not yet been established and that no arrests had been made.
In the second incident, police said that a bullet-riddled vehicle was found in a semi-rural area outside the city of Pietermaritzburg in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal.
"Inside the vehicle police found eight men who had multiple gunshot wounds and were certified dead at the scene," a police statement said.
Police said they were also still trying to determine a motive and were working to identify the victims.

"We have seen these kinds of shootings before and there have been different motives from stock theft-related, to drugs-related to taxi violence," KwaZulu-Natal province police spokesman, Colonel Robert Netshiunda, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.
Gunmen kill 27 in two shootings in South Africa
South Africa's high rates of crime
In September, at least 28 people were gunned down in mass shootings in Gauteng and the Western Cape in two of the most recent incidents.
Over the years, South Africa has consistently ranked among the countries with the world's highest murder rates, recording between 36 and 45 murders per 100,000 people annually.

The country also continues to grapple with high levels of gender-based violence, sexual violence and other contact crimes while police battle with large case loads, contibuting to low convictions rates.

articles.title: DFA chief mum on Pax Silica deal signing during Trump's PH visit
articles.summary: Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro on Monday declined to say whether an agreement on the proposed Pax Silica initiative would be signed during the upcoming visit of US President Donald…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 6:48pm

Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro on Monday declined to say whether an agreement on the proposed Pax Silica initiative would be signed during the upcoming visit of US President Donald Trump to the Philippines.

“Let me reiterate, my mandate here is to reflect on the meetings that happened today. If there’s any question on diplomatic state-to-state Philippine discussions, then we’ll wait for that day, or perhaps we just have to have the discussions first,” Lazaro said in a press conference on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.
“Because I’m doing it on a day-to-day basis,” she added.

US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton earlier said there was no scheduled announcement on the Pax Silica initiative during the ASEAN Summit. He said decisions would be made in “full consultation with the government of the Philippines at the appropriate time.”
Students and progressive groups have staged several protests against the proposed initiative ahead of Trump's arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday, November 17.
Malacañang, meanwhile, urged students to submit a position paper and discuss their concerns with the government regarding the proposed Pax Silica initiative with the United States.

Earlier this month, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) said there was no specific date yet for the signing of the legal framework for the planned Pax Silica initiative, which was initially targeted for November, coinciding with Trump's visit to the Philippines.

An official from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), meanwhile, said the legal framework for Pax Silica was still expected to be signed by the Philippine and US governments before the end of 2026.
No talks about protests
Lazaro also said President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. and other members of the Philippine delegation had not discussed the protests amid the ASEAN Summit.

“No. The ASEAN was talking about regional issues. The President or no one from the Philippine delegation is talking about anything domestic,” she said when asked whether concerns had been raised about the protests.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Polish police arrest 3 teens over suspected neo-Nazi terror plot
articles.summary: Investigators found information sharing on how to make explosives at home as well as chemicals needed for that purpose.

image.caption: The three were arrested by security officials [FILE: October 2014]Image: Leszek Szymanski/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Three teenagers have been arrested in Poland on suspicion of planning a terror attack, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland's special services, said in a post on social media on Wednesday.
The suspects, a 16-year-old and two 17-year-olds, allegedly had links to an international neo-Nazi movement.
The arrest comes days after a gunman with reported far-right leanings opened fire in Krakow, killing six people.
What do we know about the suspected neo-Nazi terror plot?
Siemoniak said in his post on X that the three teenagers had been arrested by the officials of the Internal Security Agency (ABW).
"The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had already begun taking steps toward committing terrorist offenses," he said.
During a search, ABW agents discovered chemicals used to make explosives, according to the minister.

The suspects were also found to have exchanged information over messaging platforms on how to make explosives, firearms and pyrotechnics at home, with the intended use of carrying out a terror attack.
The two 17-year-olds have been taken into pre-trial detention, with the 16-year-old being sent to a juvenile detention facility, Siemoniak said.
Poland mourns victims of Krakow mass shooting
Poland is on high alert after 24-year-old Michal Oksinski killed six people and injured 15 more when he started shooting on Krakow's Main Market Square on November 7.
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said Oksinski had been fascinated with Norwegian neo-Nazi mass killer Anders Breivik and had amassed a large amount of ammunition before his rampage.

articles.title: US and Russia to oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons
articles.summary: 'The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies — including autonomous weapon systems — present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges,' UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres…

blocks.text: ANTONIO GUTERRES. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres speaks during a press conference on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Pasay City, Philippines, November 16, 2026.
Eloisa Lopez/Reuters

'The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies — including autonomous weapon systems — present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges,' UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres says

items: The US and Russia are expected to oppose negotiations for legally binding rules on autonomous weapons at a UN meeting in Geneva, despite support from most of the 128 states involved.
The rise of AI in military technology has raised ethical concerns, with calls for regulation to prevent machines from making life-and-death decisions on the battlefield.
The discussions are anticipated to be challenging, with various options on the table, including legally binding and non-binding agreements, as well as a potential compromise.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

GENEVA, Switzerland – Major arms producers the United States and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting in Geneva this week to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, in what diplomats and rights groups expect to be difficult talks.

The rise of artificial intelligence has boosted development of drones, robots, tanks, submarines and other military hardware capable of killing without human involvement. Semi-autonomous, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan, and the Middle East, despite ethical concerns.

The UN-hosted meeting starting on Monday, November 16, is due to decide whether to launch negotiations for a legally binding agreement on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS).

But while most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons support that, major military nations including the US, Russia and Israel oppose it, arguing that existing humanitarian law is sufficient.

As talks opened in Geneva on Monday, the UN secretary-general urged states via video message to agree to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument to regulate autonomous weapon systems, including clear prohibitions and restrictions.
“The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies – including autonomous weapon systems – present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges,” Antonio Guterres said in a statement.

blocks.caption: UN and Red Cross call for urgent rules on autonomous weapons

blocks.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross, along with the pope, has also warned of the dangers from autonomous weapons and support regulation.

“Machines should never be allowed to decide who lives and dies on a battlefield but that is the dystopian reality that is fast approaching,” said Verity Coyle from Human Rights Watch, which is urging the Review Conference to take firm action.

Two diplomats told Reuters the discussions looked set to be challenging. But states could build bridges to find a compromise agreement by the end of the week, they said. All options are on the table, from legally binding to non-legally binding, as well as a hybrid agreement with both elements, one of the diplomats added.
Campaigners say autonomous weapons systems can behave unpredictably, raising the risk of fatal errors.

Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute – a US-based nonprofit organization focused on reducing the risks of advanced technologies, including AI – said LAWS were no longer science fiction, pointing to media reporting of early use of fully autonomous systems in Ukraine.

The US favors guidelines over binding rules on LAWS, arguing that international law already provides a framework to govern warfare. It has proposed a five-year mandate for talks towards a non-binding agreement.
The Red Cross says humanitarian law does not sufficiently address specific risks from autonomous weapons.

Russia has not publicly stated its position going into the talks, but has previously resisted proposals for a legally binding agreement. It plans to block the European Union, an observer to the talks, from taking the floor, a senior Western diplomat told Reuters.
Hehir told Reuters the US and Russia would probably seek to water down any outcome as they did in September with a text about autonomous weapons and their potential for harm.
The chair of this week’s talks has proposed a two-year mandate to negotiate a legally binding protocol.
The UK, Germany, and France propose negotiations on an instrument that leaves open whether it would be legally binding or not, Coyle told Reuters. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DFA on 80% COC completion: I don't think its a failure
articles.summary: The DFA said reaching 80% completion on the South China Sea Code of Conduct is not a "failure," and that the Philippines has done what it can under its chairmanship of the ASEAN.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 6:45pm

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Monday said reaching 80% completion on the South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) is not a "failure," and that the Philippines has done what it can under its chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit given the time period.

"We have done 80% or more than that. So I don't think it's a failure. I think we have done what we have to do as far as Philippines as chair," DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said in a press briefing on Monday.
"But we did have more time. I don't know what's wrong with that," she added.

Lazaro reiterated that the COC failed to reach its completion under the Philippines' chairmanship due to time constraints in the negotiations. She earlier said that the COC will be completed in 2027, during Singapore's turn as ASEAN chair.
"It's just that we lack material time. If we were given another five to six months, we could have finished it," she said.
China and Malaysia currently chair the COC negotiations until mid-2027, then China and Lao will chair it for the remainder of the year.

The proposed code seeks to establish rules to prevent disputes in the South China Sea from escalating and developing into a major armed conflict that could involve the United States, a Philippine ally, and other countries in the region.
The Philippines will pass its ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore.
"To say that it will finish for 2027. Now, we give it to Singapore probably under the way they're shepherding the whole thing," Lazaro said.
"But I don't think I can give you a timeline as to when the Code of Conduct will finish," she added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Birth keeper told mother of baby who later died to ‘go home and rest’, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births

  • Get our

blocks.text: A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.
The inquest will examine whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth.

Baby R’s mother had a distrust of hospitals in general, the court heard. She was aligned with and trusted Kali. She felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to the baby. In a police statement she said she felt threatened by her experiences at the hospital.

At 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that the baby was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent. She was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth, the inquest heard.
She called Kali, who said in a police statement, “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do.”
Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. Two doulas were in attendance; neither had medical training. The baby was white in colour. He never latched on to feed.
About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The cause of his death was determined to be unascertained. But an expert neonatologist surmised that it was caused by hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy resulting from severe post-maturity – being born at 43 weeks.
Prof Hannah Dahlen, a midwifery academic who has attended thousands of births, told the court that this was a baby “I would have been watching closely” as a midwife attending a birth.
after newsletter promotion

She said the difference between a doula and a birthing midwife “is the theoretical knowledge that we add on to that clinical experience, which gives us an understanding and an ability to interpret signs and symptoms and to identify what pathology is going on, or what physiology is not actually working at this time and making a decision”.

The counsel assisting, Ragni Mathur, told the court women were choosing unregulated free birthing because of “traumatic or coercive experiences, fragmented care, lack of trust in clinicians, lack of available clinicians, lack of services in regional NSW, and including child protection notifications and regulatory actions against new lives”.

articles.title: Electric or shock: COP31 is having an electric moment
articles.summary: A key pledge at COP31 seeks to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption needs to 35% by 2035

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Surging energy costs due to the conflict in the Middle East have created momentum for clean energy transition and total phaseout of fossil fuels.

The presidency of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, wants to set the global objective: the 35×35 Global Electrification Pledge, a collective ambition to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption needs from 23% in 2026 to 35% by 2035.
“Nations now face a choice: electric or shock,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said during the first week of COP.
“Rewire the global economy for the electricity age,” said Stiell. “Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms, and national budgets.”
Meanwhile, civil society groups continue their call on governments and world leaders to phase out fossil fuels.
In the Philippines where the 49th ASEAN summit is happening simultaneously with COP31 in Turkey, climate groups are urging ASEAN leaders to raise the ambitions in their electrification agenda.
“Our region is on fire, and we have a moral responsibility to act now,” Bishop Gerry Alminaza, a Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines’ climate champion, said on Monday, November 16.
The International Renewable Energy Agency has estimated that renewable energy sources in the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand enabled savings of “around $5.7 billion in coal and gas purchases.”

Parallel to these electrification efforts is the call to phase out fossil fuels. At the COP30 in Brazil, there was strong opposition from oil-producing countries to include a fossil fuel phaseout roadmap in its final decision.
This was met by strong criticisms from many delegates and climate champions.
Things have changed since the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and the Strait of Hormuz was blocked. A global oil crisis has since caused economic shocks in most countries.
The impact has been felt by households. In the Philippines, demand for solar panels for their homes have gone up.
Now there is a renewed appreciation on Brazil’s roadmap.
“COP31 sent a clear signal: the days of coal, oil and gas are numbered,” said Bruce Douglas of the Global Renewables Alliance, in a statement on Sunday, November 15.
“Brazil’s roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels and growing support for electrification are building momentum to end that dependence.”
Brazil recently formally handed over its fossil fuel transition roadmap to the COP31 presidency.

“We must leave Antalya with a clear understanding of the next steps to advance this roadmap, and I encourage the current and future COP presidencies to carry this work forward,” said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres during the turnover on November 11.
Countries, development banks, and private finance firms recently launched the Electrify Now Finance Coalition. It will run until COP33 in 2028.
The World Bank Group and the African Development Bank co-chair the coalition.
“This coalition will help developing countries build strong project pipelines and attract the investment they need,” COP31 Presidency Murat Kurum said in a statement.
“This is how COP31 is starting a new era of electrification.” (READ: COP31 leaders try out new sales pitch for climate action: Do it for the economy)
Finance is a sticky topic during these climate summits. Climate targets of developing nations are reliant on external support.
Stiell has noted that the global energy transition is uneven “and many nations need much more support to get fully on board.”

articles.title: SC raises compensation for crime victims, citing inflation, severity of offenses
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has increased the monetary awards for crime victims, taking into account the gravity of offenses, the suffering endured by victims and survivors, and economic realities such as…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 6:24pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has increased the monetary awards for crime victims, taking into account the gravity of offenses, the suffering endured by victims and survivors, and economic realities such as inflation.

In a press release on Monday, the SC En Banc announced that it had approved updated guidelines governing the award of civil indemnity ex delicto, moral damages, exemplary damages and temperate damages.

“The value of judicial awards should not remain fixed when the financial and social circumstances underlying them have materially changed. Inflation, cost of living, wage growth, and fiscal stability are relevant considerations in determining appropriate awards,” the SC said.

However, the Court stressed that the review should not be reduced to a mere computation of inflation, noting that damages in criminal cases involving violations of bodily integrity, dignity and personal autonomy cannot be measured solely in monetary terms.
Under the new guidelines, the Court increased the civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages awarded to a child victim who was six years old when the crimes were committed.
The awards were raised as follows:

items: Qualified rape of a minor: P325,000 each, from P100,000
Acts of lasciviousness: P175,000 each, from P50,000

blocks.text: The awards will also earn 6% annual legal interest from the finality of the decision until full payment, the SC said.

Trial courts are also required to direct the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) to refer child victims, with the consent of their guardians, to a Rape Crisis Center for care and support.
The High Court said judges retain the discretion to increase the compensation further, depending on the circumstances of each case.

For crimes resulting in death, the SC set the highest compensation ranges, recognizing that the loss of life is permanent and irreversible. It also established higher baseline awards for intentional killings than for deaths caused by negligence.
The Court ruled that all awards for civil indemnity, moral damages, exemplary damages and temperate damages in criminal cases must follow the updated amounts under the new guidelines.

The amounts will be determined based on the “penalty prescribed by law, the nature and stage of consummation of the offense, the extent of injury or loss, and the lived experience of the victim and survivors.”

“Civil damages are not merely incidental relief in criminal proceedings. They are essential expressions of the law’s recognition of the harm suffered by victims and society’s condemnation of criminal conduct,” the SC said.
Through the updated guidelines, the Court seeks to ensure that monetary awards remain consistent, proportionate to the gravity of offenses and responsive to victims' circumstances, it added.
The ruling was penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Jordan bans Telegram app over 'radicalisation' claims
articles.summary: Jordan has imposed a ban on Telegram over a deadly church attack which left seven people dead. The kingdom claims that content on the messaging app poses a threat to "national interests."

image.caption: Telegram currently boasts over a billion usersImage: IMAGO

blocks.text: Jordan on Monday announced a ban on instant messaging service Telegram after a deadly attack on a church last month.
Jordan's ‌Public ⁠Security Directorate said the move aimed to protect the society from "the attempts to spread extremism and radicalisation."
All of which pose a "threat to societal security and national interests," it said.
In December 2022, Jordan also banned TikTok over videos authorities claimed "promoted killing and chaos."
What prompted the ban?
The ban on Telegram comes after a shooting on October 23 at a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Karak governate which left seven people dead and another 34 wounded.

Jordan, in retaliation, organised airstrikes on neighbouring Syria and said it had killed 20 so-called "Islamic State" militants. The government also acknowledged that a number of civilians had been killed in the strikes.
A Jordanian court sentenced three men to death by hanging on Sunday in connection with the attack. Authorities identified them as "followers of a hardline Islamist ideology."

blocks.caption: The Jordanian government said last month that a number of civilians had been killed in airstrikes on neighboring SyriaImage: Khalil Ashawi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state and close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.
Christians make up around 3% of Jordan's population of 10 million. The Levantine country is home to one of the oldest Christian communities in the world.
Telegram and 'IS'
Over the years, so-called "Islamic State" militants have used Telegram for propaganda and communication purposes.
The Russian-born billionaire Pavel Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013.
Middle East conflicts take toll on Jordan's tourism sector
In July, Russia ‌said it had charged him with "aiding terrorist activities," accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.
Durov rejects the allegations, arguing that Telegram has gone "beyond its obligations in moderating content and assisting authorities in tackling crime."
He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.

articles.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
articles.summary:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a…

blocks.text: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

blocks.caption: The City of Cape Town says the troop was relocated due to the ‘severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment’. Photograph: Nardus Engelbrecht/AP

blocks.text: It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

blocks.caption: Animal rights activists disagree on how best to handle the boom in baboon populations in Cape Town. Photograph: Nardus Engelbrecht/AP

blocks.text: The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

articles.title: Teodoro confident US would help PH if South China Sea tension escalates
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday expressed confidence that the US would honor its treaty commitments to the Philippines in case tensions escalate in the South China Sea.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 5:51pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Monday expressed confidence that the United States would honor its treaty commitments to the Philippines in case tensions escalate in the South China Sea (SCS).

“As of now, I have no reason to doubt. So it's a yes. But of course, that is conditioned on the fact that we don't do anything stupid, right?” Teodoro said at the Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea.
“I mean, we don't do anything that any country would object to, any right-minded and reasonable-minded country wouldn't object to. And that's vice versa,” he added.
Teodoro said the Philippines is also working with the US to prevent a potential clash in the SCS through stronger defense cooperation.
“We are here working together precisely on a defense basis to prevent the time when the time comes that, you know, the inevitable clash happens,” he said.
However, he said the Philippines would be more optimistic if there were a collective parity of potential force to serve as a backstop.
“I am optimistic. However, I will be more optimistic if there is a collective parity of potential force as a backstop. Anybody needs a backbone,” he said.

“If not, you have a wheelchair. So, even if you engage in anything, I think it's fundamental that we need a backbone. That backbone is resiliency. And unfortunately, as history has proved, a solid defense footing is really required for your national resilience,” he said.
Meanwhile, Teodoro said the Philippines cannot rely on China's goodwill in dealing with the proposed ASEAN-China Code of Conduct in the disputed waters.

"To see is to believe, and I will reserve my opinion on trust. I am not to rely on the good faith of an adversary. If I rely on the good faith of an adversary in my job as defense secretary, then they might as well find somebody else," he said.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. — BM, GMA News
